item.title: Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking: where contractor insurance lives in Forma Build and what it checks
item.description: Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking, mapped for Forma Build: compliance requirements on contracts and pay apps, expiration dates, TradeTapp and what it skips.
item.content:encoded:
• Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking lives in Cost Management in Forma Build. Project admins set compliance requirements, such as a certificate of insurance with an expiration date, on contracts, payment applications and change orders, and the item can't be submitted until they're met.
  • TradeTapp, Autodesk's prequalification tool, can add a condition that blocks sending a contract when a supplier's insurance documents are missing or expired. Autodesk's docs describe uploading and dating documents, not reading what the endorsements say.

This is the second post in our "What's in your stack" series, where we take one tool general contractors run every day and show where contractor insurance and COI data sits in it. Last time it was Procore. This time it's Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking, which now lives under a new name.

In March 2026, Autodesk said Autodesk Construction Cloud is now Autodesk Forma. Autodesk Build became Forma Build, and Autodesk Docs became Forma Data Management. Autodesk says nothing moved: no data migration, and no change to URLs, logins, APIs or integrations. So if your team still says "ACC," the setup below is the one you have.

Every Autodesk detail below comes from Autodesk's own pages and help docs, checked on Nov 26, 2026. Check the linked page before you change a setup.

Can Autodesk Construction Cloud track certificates of insurance?

Yes, Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking runs through compliance requirements in Cost Management, part of Forma Build. Autodesk's compliance requirements help page says the workflow can "track and store lien waivers, certificates of insurance, bonding documents, and other required materials before submissions proceed."

Project administrators create compliance requirement templates in settings, on the Cost or Change Order tab. Members with collaborative permission then upload the documents on each item, from their computer or from Forma Data Management. For certificates of insurance and other time-sensitive documents, the requirement can ask for an expiration date, and Autodesk says expired documents show in calendar views and notifications.

Where does contractor insurance data live in Forma Build?

Contractor insurance data in Forma Build lives on the cost items that compliance requirements attach to, and in TradeTapp if you use it for qualification.

Where contractor insurance lives in Autodesk Forma
WhereAttaches toWhat it holdsCan it block?
Cost Management, document-based compliance requirementContracts, cost payment applications, subcontract change orders, owner change orders, RFQsThe uploaded certificate and, if required, its expiration dateYes, Submit stays disabled until required documents are uploaded; it can be unblocked
Cost Management, TradeTapp condition (Insurance Programme)ContractsWhether the supplier's insurance documents in TradeTapp are present and not expiredYes, sending the contract is blocked; members can't override it on the contract
TradeTapp qualification recordThe subcontractor, across projectsQuestionnaire answers, internal limits, qualification status and expirationThrough the contract condition above

Each item shows a compliance status: Compliant, Pending (documents needed), Not Applicable or Not Required. A requirement can be made optional, and if every requirement on an item is optional, Autodesk counts the item as compliant.

Notice what the record doesn't hold: limits, policy numbers or carriers as typed fields, the way some systems store certificates of insurance. Compliance requirements in Forma Build track that the right document is uploaded and dated. They don't store what it says.

How do compliance requirements block a contract or payment application?

Compliance requirements block a contract or payment application by disabling submission until they're met. Autodesk says the system "can block submissions until requirements are met," and a required document keeps the Submit button disabled until it's uploaded.

That makes a certificate of insurance requirement on a cost payment application the closest thing Forma Build has to holding a payment for missing insurance. Two details matter:

  1. Document-based blocks can be lifted. Autodesk says "you can unblock and allow submission actions even when compliance is pending." Decide who on your team may do that, and when.
  2. TradeTapp blocks can't. A TradeTapp-based condition always blocks sending the contract when it isn't met, and members can't override it on the contract.

If subcontractors bill through GCPay, Autodesk's GCPay integration page says they complete the compliance documents the general contractor asks for there, and approved payment applications come into Cost Management read-only. The page doesn't say the compliance documents themselves sync.

What does TradeTapp add for insurance?

TradeTapp adds a check on insurance before the contract goes out. TradeTapp is Autodesk's qualification tool, with custom questionnaires, internal limits, financial ratio calculations, approval workflows, project-specific assessments and automated renewal requests to subcontractors. It syncs qualification data to BuildingConnected Pro, where Autodesk's bid management post shows qualification status, expiration date and project and total limits next to each bidder.

The link to Cost Management is the Insurance Programme condition: if the supplier's insurance documents in TradeTapp are missing or expired, the contract can't be sent. That's a useful gate at award. It checks presence and date, not coverage, and TradeTapp's own page doesn't describe reading certificates or endorsements.

What doesn't Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking check?

Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking checks that a certificate is uploaded and, if you ask, that it's in date. The help pages we read don't describe reading the certificate, pulling limits from it, or checking the endorsements behind it. None of them mention additional insured forms, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory wording, or completed operations.

That's where the risk sits on a contractor COI. A certificate can be uploaded, dated and Compliant in Forma Build while the umbrella limit is below the subcontract, or the additional insured endorsement covers ongoing operations and not completed operations. Our guide to endorsement review explains why the form, not the checkbox, decides coverage, and how to check a contractor COI walks through each line someone still has to read.

Requirements for certificates of insurance are also set per project, in project settings. If an owner on one job wants higher limits than your standard, the requirement can say so in its name or description, but checking the document against it is a person's job.

Where does contractor insurance and COI data sit in Autodesk Forma?

Contractor insurance and COI data in Autodesk Forma sits in Cost Management, as uploaded documents with expiration dates on contracts, payment applications and change orders, and in TradeTapp, as qualification records that can stop a contract from being sent. The certificate is a file. The date is a field. The coverage inside it isn't checked by anything in Autodesk's docs.

That makes Autodesk Construction Cloud COI tracking in Forma Build a good place to enforce that a current certificate is on file before a contract goes out or a payment application moves, and a good record of who uploaded what. It isn't, by itself, a reviewer of what the certificate and endorsements say. Teams fill that gap with a person on the risk or project team, or with a tool connected to Autodesk. If you're weighing tools, use our COI tracking software checklist and see how they compare in our guide to the best COI tracking software for construction. Autodesk's pricing page doesn't list prices, so ask your rep whether Cost Management and TradeTapp are in your contract.

item.title: Best COI compliance platform for insurance brokers and general contractors to work together (2026)
item.description: The best COI compliance platform for insurance brokers and general contractors depends on broker access: reselling a tool to clients, or working inside the GC's project.
item.content:encoded:
• COI compliance platforms work with insurance brokers in two ways: the broker resells or refers a tool to clients, or the broker works inside the general contractor's project on each gap. Most broker programs are the first kind.
  • For collaboration on a job, the test is what the broker sees. If the broker gets the project requirements, the deficiency and the project together, the fix comes back right the first time.
  • None of the broker program pages we read publish a fee, a revenue share or what the broker can see. Ask for all three in writing, and keep approvals with the general contractor.

Insurance brokers who write construction spend a lot of the week between two parties: the contractor client who needs to start work, and the general contractor whose compliance tool says the certificate falls short. When both sides work from the same COI compliance platform, a gap can close in one round. When they don't, it turns into an email thread.

This guide is for producers and account managers at agencies that write contractors and general contractors. It explains the two ways COI compliance platforms work with insurance brokers, names the platforms on each side with each vendor's own page linked and a screenshot of it, and gives five questions to ask before you recommend one or sign up. It isn't a scored ranking, because the platforms do different jobs.

Forsured makes a COI compliance platform that general contractors use and brokers work in, so read it knowing that. It's listed below with the others, and we say where other tools fit better.

What is the best COI compliance platform for insurance brokers to collaborate with general contractors?

The best COI compliance platform for insurance brokers to collaborate with general contractors is one where the broker works inside the general contractor's project: the broker sees the project requirements, the deficiency and the document together, uploads the fix in the same place, and the general contractor approves. That's the model Forsured is built on.

If what you want is a tool to offer your own clients, resold or referred, the broker programs at TrustLayer, illumend, Billy and Certificial fit better. Those are a different job, and many agencies end up doing both.

What are the two ways a COI compliance platform works with insurance brokers?

A COI compliance platform works with insurance brokers in one of two ways.

  1. The broker offers the platform to clients. The agency resells or refers a tracking tool to a client, often a general contractor or property owner, who then tracks their own vendors' certificates. The broker earns revenue or a client discount and becomes the client's guide to the tool. This is what most published broker programs describe.
  2. The broker works inside the general contractor's project. The general contractor already runs the platform. When a contractor's certificate falls short, the contractor's broker, or the general contractor's own broker, is brought into that project to fix it. This is collaboration on the job, and it's where most of a broker's certificate time goes.

The two models answer different questions. The first is "what can I sell or recommend?" The second is "how do I get this contractor cleared on this project today?" A COI deficiency notice is the second kind of problem, and it's the one this guide puts first.

Which COI compliance platform fits which kind of broker access?

Each COI compliance platform below gives insurance brokers a different kind of broker access. Here's what each vendor's own page says, checked Nov 25, 2026.

Forsured: best for working inside the general contractor's project

Forsured is built for general contractors, with insurance brokers working in the same workflow. Its homepage describes a shared general contractor and broker resolution workflow: the general contractor sends the gap to the broker, and the broker sees the requirement, the document and the project, so the fix comes back right. For brokers, the homepage lists seeing the project requirements for each project and why a submission needs attention. Forsured is onboarding a limited number of general contractors and broker partners at a time, and it doesn't publish a broker resale program.

![The Forsured homepage, showing a sample contractor checked against project requirements with two gaps flagged and the broker fixing both](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-compliance-platform-brokers-general-contractors/shot-forsured.png "forsured.ai homepage, checked Nov 25, 2026")

TrustLayer: best for agencies that want to resell a platform and offer review services

TrustLayer runs a partner program for agencies. Its brokers page says partners can earn revenue by reselling the software and offering review services, lists a partner portal, a channel account manager and referral opportunities, and says any agency that specializes in property and casualty insurance can join. On the project side, TrustLayer says subcontractors upload certificates directly, all parties can review them in the platform, and it doesn't approve a certificate without input from the broker and their client. The page doesn't publish partner terms.

![The TrustLayer page for brokers and partners](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-compliance-platform-brokers-general-contractors/shot-trustlayer.png "TrustLayer brokers and partners page, checked Nov 25, 2026")

illumend: best for referring clients who want AI to make the call

illumend, from myCOI, runs a referral program for insurance brokers. Its broker page offers a co-branded referral page, talking points and a referral-only client discount, and says clients run the tracking themselves, "not by you." Its homepage says its AI reads the documents and makes the compliance decision, with a reviewer stepping in on items it can't resolve. The page doesn't describe broker access to a client's account or the client's project requirements.

![The illumend page for insurance brokers](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-compliance-platform-brokers-general-contractors/shot-illumend.png "illumend broker partner page, checked Nov 25, 2026")

Billy: best for an agency-branded tool for construction clients

Billy offers insurance brokers and carriers agency-branded COI tracking software for construction clients, and says agencies can create revenue through compliance review services. Its product features include certificate deficiency highlights and non-compliant notes. The page doesn't describe broker access or partner terms. On a project, Billy's FAQ says vendors and their brokers upload through a secure link with no account.

![The Billy page for brokers and carriers](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-compliance-platform-brokers-general-contractors/shot-billy.png "Billy brokers and carriers page, checked Nov 25, 2026")

Certificial: best for brokers who issue on a network

Certificial works from the issuing side. Its Agent Assist program lets agencies help clients track their own vendors' certificates and says agents can earn additional revenue from it. Agencies that join its network issue certificates that stay current for the holder, and its agents page says the network is free for agents, brokers and carriers. It fits brokers who want their own certificates to arrive right, more than collaboration inside a general contractor's project.

![The Certificial Agent Assist program page](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-compliance-platform-brokers-general-contractors/shot-certificial.png "Certificial Agent Assist page, checked Nov 25, 2026")

Jones: best for owners and property managers who coordinate with vendors' agents

Jones lists insurance brokers and consultants as an audience and describes a vendor and broker engagement hub that coordinates directly with vendors and insurance agents to resolve missing documents. The same file says it's typically billed per tenant or vendor record per property, so it fits brokers whose clients own or manage buildings as well as build them.

![The Jones homepage, headed Insurance Compliance For The Built World](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-compliance-platform-brokers-general-contractors/shot-jones.png "getjones.com homepage, checked Nov 25, 2026")

For how these and other tools compare from the general contractor's side, see our alternatives to myCOI, TrustLayer and Jones.

How do the platforms compare on project requirements and approvals?

None of these pages publishes a referral fee, a revenue share or a broker price beyond Certificial's free tier, so ask.

How should insurance brokers choose a COI compliance platform?

Insurance brokers should choose a COI compliance platform by asking five questions, in this order. The CFMA's Austin chapter makes the same case for collaboration among builders, brokers and carriers: compliance works when each party sees the same data.

  1. Which model is it? A tool you resell to clients, or a workspace inside the general contractor's project? Many agencies need both, from different vendors.
  2. What does broker access show? You want the project requirements, the exact deficiency, the document that failed and the project. A notice that only says "noncompliant" costs you a second round. Our guide to how a GC checks a contractor COI shows what they're reading for.
  3. Who invites the broker, and to what? Broker access should come from the general contractor or the contractor client, and cover only the projects or contractors you serve.
  4. Who approves? The broker fixes; the general contractor decides. Know whether a person or AI makes the call.
  5. Who pays, and what do you earn? Get any fee, revenue share or client discount in writing, because the pages don't say.

item.title: COI deficiency notice tools for insurance brokers (2026): what helps you answer faster
item.description: Tools that help insurance brokers answer a COI deficiency notice: agency management systems, certificate networks, outsourcing and the GC's own portal, compared.
item.content:encoded:
• Most COI deficiency notices ask for an endorsement or a higher limit. A corrected certificate can't add coverage, so the fix starts with the policy, and the certificate follows.
  • Your agency management system issues the corrected certificate. Certificate networks and client self-service cut the volume, and outsourced certificate teams take the overflow.
  • The general contractor's own tool decides how fast the fix lands. Ask for the exact requirement, the project and where to upload, so you answer once instead of three times.

A COI deficiency notice lands in an account manager's inbox the same way every time: a general contractor, or the compliance tool they use, says a contractor client's certificate doesn't meet the project. The client wants it fixed today, because they can't start work or get paid until it is. Multiply that by every contractor client on every job, and certificate work becomes a big share of the week for insurance brokers who write construction.

This guide is for commercial lines account managers and producers at agencies with contractor clients. It covers the tools that help you answer a COI deficiency notice faster, grouped by the job each one does, with each vendor's own page linked and a screenshot of it. It isn't a ranking, because the tools do different jobs and most agencies use more than one.

Forsured makes compliance software that general contractors use and brokers work in, so read it knowing that. Forsured is one of the general contractor's tools listed below, with its limits.

What tools help insurance brokers respond to a COI deficiency notice?

The tools that help insurance brokers respond to a COI deficiency notice fall into four groups: your agency management system, which issues the corrected certificate; a certificate network, which keeps issued certificates current; an outsourced certificate team, which takes the volume; and the general contractor's own compliance tool, which is where the notice came from and where the fix has to land.

None of them fixes the most common problem on its own. That's because most notices aren't certificate problems.

What does a COI deficiency notice usually ask for?

A COI deficiency notice usually asks for coverage, not paperwork: an additional insured endorsement, often both ongoing and completed operations, a waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory wording, or a higher limit. Certificates miss often. IA Magazine cited industry estimates that 45% to 55% of initial COI submissions are rejected for errors or missing information.

So before you open any tool, sort the notice into one of two piles:

  1. The coverage is on the policy, and the certificate didn't show it. The holder name is wrong, the endorsement wasn't attached, or the description of operations is missing the project. A corrected certificate fixes this, usually the same day.
  2. The coverage isn't on the policy. The endorsement was never added, or the limit is below the subcontract. No certificate can fix this. It's a conversation with the client and the carrier first, and a certificate isn't coverage on its own.

Most delay comes from mixing the two up: a corrected certificate goes back, the general contractor rejects it again, and the email thread grows. The fastest tools are the ones that show you the exact requirement and the project, so you know which pile you're in on the first read. Our guide to how a GC checks a contractor COI shows what they're reading for.

Which tools fit which job?

Each group of tools fits a different part of the job. Here's what each vendor's own page says, checked Nov 24, 2026.

Applied Epic and Applied CSR24: best for issuing the corrected certificate from your agency management system

Your agency management system is where the corrected certificate gets issued. Applied Systems describes issuing certificates to holders from Applied Epic, and Applied CSR24 lets you issue a certificate for a single holder from a template, add holder-specific endorsements, resend earlier certificates and email up to three recipients. Agencies on Applied Epic can import attachments into CSR24, which is how an endorsement travels with the certificate.

![The Applied CSR24 help page on issuing a certificate for a single holder](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-applied.png "Applied CSR24 help page, checked Nov 24, 2026")

Vertafore AgencyOne Certificates: best for certificates from live agency data

Vertafore announced on Apr 16, 2026 that its Certificates tool in AgencyOne uses real-time data from the agency management system, and that clients can generate and get certificates on their own through InsurLink. They say it's available to AgencyOne customers with AMS360 and InsurLink, with Sagitta coming later in 2026.

![The Vertafore press release announcing the Certificates tool in AgencyOne](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-vertafore.png "Vertafore press release, checked Nov 24, 2026")

Certificial: best for certificates that stay current

Certificial runs a network where an agent issues a certificate once and the holder always has the current one. Their agents page lists requirement comparison, insured self-service, automatic distribution and endorsement management, and says they connect to agency management systems. It says the network is "completely free for Agents, Brokers and Carriers," and the same page also lists Premium and Enterprise plans at $249 and $639 a year.

The Big I, the independent agents' trade association, has cautioned agents about third-party requests that ask for policy data in place of a certificate. Read what any network asks you to share before you join.

![The Certificial page for agents and brokers](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-certificial.png "Certificial agents and brokers page, checked Nov 24, 2026")

ReSource Pro Certs Center: best for handing off certificate volume

ReSource Pro offers Certs Center, an outsourced certificate service for agencies, on a pay-per-use model based on volume. They say it standardizes the workflow and quote on-demand turnaround of one to two hours. It takes the issuing off your desk. Deciding whether a client needs a new endorsement stays with you.

![The ReSource Pro page for its outsourced certificate of insurance services for agencies](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-resource-pro.png "ReSource Pro Certs Center page, checked Nov 24, 2026")

The general contractor's own tool: best for sending the fix where it counts

The notice usually comes from the general contractor's compliance tool, and how that tool works decides how many rounds it takes. Three examples:

  • Forsured puts the deficiency in a shared workspace where the broker sees the requirement, the document and the project, and a person on the GC's team approves or waives each result.
  • Billy sends a request email, and its FAQ says vendors and their brokers upload through a secure link with no account. It tells a vendor to send the deficiency list to the broker, who "can usually issue a corrected certificate the same day."
  • TrustLayer lets subcontractors upload directly, sends expiration notices and follow-ups to subs and their brokers, and says it doesn't approve a certificate without input from the broker and their client.

![The Forsured homepage, showing a sample contractor checked against project requirements with two gaps flagged](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-forsured.png "forsured.ai homepage, checked Nov 24, 2026")

![The Billy FAQ page](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-billy.png "Billy FAQ page, checked Nov 24, 2026")

![The TrustLayer article on how it works with brokers](https://forsured.ai/blog/coi-deficiency-notice-tools-brokers/shot-trustlayer.png "TrustLayer broker article, checked Nov 24, 2026")

How do the tools compare?

The tools compare on what job they do and who pays for them. The general contractor's tools are paid for by the general contractor.

How should an agency set up its COI deficiency workflow?

Set up your COI deficiency workflow so that every notice gets sorted, answered once and closed where the general contractor will see it. Insurance brokers who do this the same way every time spend less of the week on rework.

  1. Ask for the requirement, not just the notice. Get the project's insurance requirements and the subcontract section the notice points to. If the GC's tool shows them, work from there.
  2. Sort it. Is the coverage on the policy and missing from the certificate, or missing from the policy? Only the first is a corrected certificate.
  3. Fix the coverage first. Add the endorsement or raise the limit with the carrier, then issue the corrected certificate with the endorsement attached from your agency management system.
  4. Answer where the notice came from. Upload to the GC's tool or link rather than replying to the email, so the item clears.
  5. Template what repeats. Save holder-specific endorsements and certificate templates for general contractors you see often, so the next COI deficiency notice from them takes minutes.

item.title: COI tracking spreadsheet, outsourced service or software: which should a GC use?
item.description: A COI tracking spreadsheet, a managed service or COI tracking software: what each catches on contractor COIs, where each breaks, and how a GC should choose.
item.content:encoded:
• A COI tracking spreadsheet tracks dates well. It can't read an endorsement or hold different requirements for each project, so a person has to do both by hand for every contractor COI.
  • When you outsource COI tracking, you buy capacity: collection, reminders and follow-up. Ask exactly what the service's reviewers read and who signs off, because the gap is still yours if it's missed.
  • COI tracking software earns its cost when requirements change by project, contractors work more than one job, and renewals pile up. Many GCs end up with software plus a person who owns the final call.

Every general contractor manages contractor COIs one of three ways: a COI tracking spreadsheet someone on the team keeps, an outside service that collects and chases for you, or COI tracking software. Most companies start with the spreadsheet, and many never question it until a certificate that looked fine turns out not to cover them.

This guide is for owners, CFOs and project executives deciding which way to go as the subcontractor list grows. It names no vendors. It compares the three on what they catch, where they break and who ends up making the call, and it says plainly when the spreadsheet is the right answer.

Forsured makes COI tracking software, so read it knowing that. The tests below work the same whichever way you choose.

Should you manage contractor COIs in a spreadsheet, outsource COI tracking, or use software?

You should manage contractor COIs in a spreadsheet only while you have a small, stable roster, one set of requirements and a person who reads every endorsement. Outsource COI tracking when the problem is capacity. Use COI tracking software when requirements change by project and contractors work more than one job, which is most general contractors past a few dozen trades.

The choice turns on two checks that catch real gaps. The first is whether each contractor COI is checked against the requirements of the project it's for, not one master list. The second is whether someone reads the endorsement itself. An additional insured is someone who isn't automatically covered by a policy, so the endorsement, not the checkbox on the certificate, is what extends coverage to you. Any of the three approaches can do both checks. They differ in who does them, how fast, and how often they get skipped.

How do the three ways compare?

The three ways compare differently on collection, requirements, endorsements and who decides. Here's the short version.

COI tracking spreadsheet, managed COI tracking service or COI tracking software: how the three compare
JobCOI tracking spreadsheetManaged COI tracking serviceCOI tracking software
Collecting certificatesYour team emails and saves filesThe service collects and chasesRequests and uploads go through the tool
Expiration datesA formula or a calendar reminderThe service sends remindersAutomatic reminders by policy
Requirements by projectOne row per policy, hard to splitDepends on how the service sets you upDepends on the tool; ask to see two projects
Reading endorsementsA person, every timeSome services do, some don'tSome tools read the wording, some only the form
Getting the broker to fix a gapYour team's emailThe service's email and callsRequests from the tool, sometimes a shared workspace
Who approvesWhoever keeps the sheetTheir reviewer, your sign-offYour team, or AI on some tools
How cost growsStaff hoursPer vendor, often with a minimumPer vendor or per plan

When is a COI tracking spreadsheet enough?

A COI tracking spreadsheet is enough when you have a short list of contractors you use again and again, your requirements barely change from job to job, and one person has the time and training to open every endorsement. In that setup the sheet is cheap, everyone knows how it works, and it holds the one thing it's built for: dates.

The problems start when any of those conditions change. Spreadsheet errors are well studied: Raymond Panko's review of the research found that spreadsheet errors are both common and non-trivial, and that cell-by-cell inspection was the one technique shown to catch them. A COI tracking spreadsheet adds a construction problem on top. It keeps one row per policy, so when two projects require different umbrella limits, the sheet can't show that a contractor passes one and fails the other. It doesn't read endorsements, so the person keeping it has to. And it doesn't notice anything. If a renewal doesn't arrive, the cell just stays the same.

Certificates also arrive wrong more often than most teams expect. IA Magazine reported that 45% to 55% of initial COI submissions are rejected for errors or missing information, according to some industry estimates. Every one of those becomes an email thread about contractor COIs that lives outside the COI tracking spreadsheet.

If you stay on a spreadsheet, keep requirements on a separate tab for each project, store the endorsement with the certificate, and have a second person spot-check approvals. Our guide to how to check a contractor COI walks through what to read on each one.

When does it make sense to outsource COI tracking?

It makes sense to outsource COI tracking when the bottleneck is hands: collecting certificates, sending reminders and chasing vendors and their brokers who don't answer. A managed COI tracking service takes that volume off your team, usually priced per vendor and often with an annual minimum.

What a service doesn't take is the risk. If a contractor turns out to be uncovered after a loss, the claim lands on your project. In one Arkansas case, a general contractor left off its contractor's policy had its own insurer pay more than $1.2 million after the Court of Appeals ruled on Mar 11, 2026 that the contractor's insurer owed nothing, Insurance Business reported. Whoever reviewed that certificate, the GC's insurer paid.

Before you outsource COI tracking, get three things in writing: what the reviewers read (certificates only, endorsements, or full policies), how your project requirements get loaded and updated, and who approves or waives a gap. Our guide to managed COI tracking services for construction lists who offers one and what each includes.

When is COI tracking software the better choice?

COI tracking software is the better choice when your projects carry their own requirements, your contractors work several jobs at once, and renewals are piling up faster than one person can track. Good software holds requirements by project, reads each contractor COI and its endorsements against them, sends the gap to the broker, and keeps watching after approval.

Not every tool does all of that. Some read endorsement wording and some only check that a form number is present, and some let AI approve on its own while others keep a person on every result. Our guide to endorsement review in COI tracking software shows the difference, and our COI tracking software checklist gives you a test for each point.

Price is rarely the deciding factor. Several tools publish free tiers or per-vendor rates, and you can see what COI tracking software costs at 50, 200 and 500 contractors before you book a demo.

Forsured checks every contractor COI against your project requirements, flags coverage gaps, brings the broker into the fix and keeps watching after approval, with a person on your team approving each result.

How do you decide for your company?

Decide by answering four questions, in this order.

  1. Do your requirements change by project? If yes, a single COI tracking spreadsheet will miss gaps. Use software, or a service that sets requirements up by project.
  2. Who reads the endorsements today? If nobody has time, either outsource COI tracking with a service that reads them, or pick software that does.
  3. How many contractor COIs renew each month? If renewals regularly slip, you need automatic requests and lapse tracking, which a sheet can't give you.
  4. Who makes the final call? Keep approvals and waivers with someone on your team, whichever way you choose.

Many general contractors land on a hybrid: COI tracking software for the work, a person who owns the decision, and a managed COI tracking service only if collection volume outgrows the team. item.title: Procore COI tracking: where contractor insurance lives in Procore and what it checks
item.description: Procore COI tracking, mapped: the Directory insurance record, project vs company insurance, Procore Pay compliance statuses, expiration emails and what it skips.
item.content:encoded:
• Procore COI tracking lives in the Directory: each insurance record holds the type, provider, policy number, limit, effective and expiration dates, a status and the certificate as an attachment, at company level or for one project.
  • Procore Pay can use those records as a payment requirement, so a commitment shows Compliant or Not Compliant before an invoice is paid. Procore's docs describe entering insurance by hand and don't describe reading endorsements.

This is the first post in our "What's in your stack" series, where we take one tool general contractors run every day and show where contractor insurance and COI data sits in it. We start with Procore COI tracking, because so many project teams already keep their vendors, commitments and invoices in Procore, and every contractor COI they collect has to land somewhere.

Every Procore detail below comes from Procore's own pages and support docs, checked on Nov 18, 2026. Procore changes its product often, and its support site notes that some pages are moving to a new version, so check the linked page before you change a setup.

Can Procore track certificates of insurance?

Yes, Procore COI tracking is built into the Directory. Each vendor's company record can carry insurance entries, and Procore's guide to adding insurance in the Company Directory lists the fields: type, insurance provider, policy number, exempt, limit amount, information received, effective date, expiration date, send expiration notification, status, notes, additional insured and attachments. The certificate itself goes in as an attachment.

So Procore insurance tracking is a structured record of what a certificate says, plus the file. A user with the Insurance Manager role types it in. Procore's docs say to enter the provider and policy number "exactly as it appears on the insurance certificate." Changes show up in the record's Change History tab, which helps when someone asks who updated a policy and when.

Where does contractor insurance data live in Procore?

Contractor insurance data in Procore lives in three places, and it helps to know which one your team actually uses.

Where contractor insurance lives in Procore
WhereLevelWhat it holdsWho keeps it current
Company Directory, insurance on the company recordAll projectsPolicy type, provider, number, limit, dates, status, notes, additional insured (free text), attachmentsInsurance managers
Project Directory, project insuranceOne projectThe same fields, for a policy or certificate that applies to that project onlyInsurance managers
Commitment, Compliance tab (Procore Pay)One commitmentInsurance compliance status: Compliant, Not Compliant, or Not Required (manual)Invoice administrators who are insurance managers or Directory admins

The company and project split matters more than it looks. Procore says to add insurance at company level "only when you want to add insurance to the company record for all projects." Project-level insurance in the Project Directory is for a single job. If one owner wants $10 million in umbrella limits and another wants $5 million, the project-level record is where that difference can show up. Our state COI requirements pages show how much the rules vary before an owner adds anything.

If you run Sage 300 CRE alongside Procore, the Procore insurance page for company records says the insurance type, effective and expiration dates, limit, name and policy number sync between the two.

How does Procore Pay use insurance compliance?

Procore Pay turns the Directory's insurance records into a status on each commitment. Procore's page on the Compliance tab on a commitment says Procore Pay "can be configured to track compliance as a payment requirement to help your team determine if an invoice is ready to pay." The tab has an Insurance card and a Contract Compliance Documents card.

There are two ways to set the insurance compliance status, per Procore's guide to insurance compliance statuses:

  1. Manual. Someone edits the commitment and picks Compliant, Not Compliant or Not Required.
  2. From the Directory. Procore manages the status for you. A commitment reads Compliant only when every listed insurance entry is Compliant, and anything else, including "Compliant - In Progress," reads Not Compliant.

Procore Pay marks a policy "Expiring Soon" starting 14 days before it expires and "Expired" from the day after. It's listed as generally available in select US markets and designed for general contractors and owner-builders. You'll need Procore Pay turned on for the company and the project, plus the Insurance Compliant payment requirement in the company-level Payments tool. Ask your Procore rep whether Procore Pay is part of your contract.

What doesn't Procore insurance tracking check?

Procore insurance tracking stores what a certificate says. Procore's own docs don't describe reading the endorsements behind it. The Additional Insured field on the project-level page is described as "a free-text entry about any additional insured entities for the Certificate of Insurance (COI)." None of the Procore pages we read mention waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory wording, or completed operations, and none describe pulling data from a certificate automatically.

That's the gap that matters on a contractor COI, and it's where Procore COI tracking needs a second step. A certificate can show the additional insured box checked while the endorsement that actually extends coverage to you is missing, or covers ongoing operations and not completed operations. Our guide to endorsement review explains why the form, not the checkbox, decides coverage, and how to check a contractor COI walks through each line.

Expiration emails are the other thing to understand. Procore sends them to insurance managers and the vendor's primary and invoice contacts based on the expiration date. Its docs say changing a status later "will NOT trigger any automated email notifications." So a policy that's still in date but missing a required endorsement won't prompt anyone on its own.

How do you set up Procore COI tracking?

Set up Procore COI tracking in this order so the records and the payment rule agree:

  1. Decide which insurance you'll keep at company level (the same on every job) and which at project level (set by an owner or contract).
  2. Give the right people the Insurance Manager role, so they can add records and receive expiration emails.
  3. For each vendor, add the policy type, provider, policy number, limit and dates exactly as the certificate shows them, check "send expiration notification," and attach the certificate and endorsements.
  4. If you use Procore Pay, turn on the Insurance Compliant payment requirement and choose the manual or Directory method for each commitment.
  5. Have someone read each contractor COI and its endorsements against the project's requirements before marking a record Compliant, since that step sits outside what Procore's docs describe.

For prequalification, Procore offers a separate Prequalification product for sending qualification forms and approving or denying submissions. Its page doesn't say what insurance details it collects, so ask how it connects to the Directory records.

Where does contractor insurance and COI data sit in Procore?

Contractor insurance and COI data in Procore sits in the Directory, on each vendor's company record or project record, and flows from there to the Compliance tab on commitments when Procore Pay is on. The certificate is an attachment. The limits and dates are typed fields. The endorsements are attachments and a free-text note, not checked items.

That makes Procore insurance records a good system of record for insurance compliance and a good place to hold a payment until the record is Compliant. It's not, by itself, a reviewer of what the endorsements say. Teams fill that gap with a person on the risk or project team, or with a tool from the Procore App Marketplace. If you're weighing tools, ask each one which Procore records it reads and writes, use our COI tracking software checklist to test them, and see how tools compare in our guide to the best COI tracking software for construction. Whichever you pick, Procore COI tracking works best when one place decides what's compliant and Procore holds the result. Procore's pricing page doesn't publish a price, so ask your rep which of these features your contract covers.

Forsured checks every contractor COI and endorsement against your project requirements, flags coverage gaps, brings the broker into the fix and keeps watching after approval, with a Procore integration available for early access customers.

item.title: COI tracking software checklist: what a general contractor should look for (12 points)
item.description: A 12-point COI tracking software checklist for general contractors: project requirements, endorsement review, the broker fix, renewals, who decides, and how to test each.
item.content:encoded:
• The first two points on any COI tracking software checklist are the ones that separate tools: requirements held by project, and endorsement review that reads the forms instead of the checkboxes.
  • Test every point with your own documents. A certificate with the additional insured box checked and no endorsement attached is the fastest way to see what a tool really reads.
  • Ask who makes the final call on each contractor COI, what's automated, and how the vendor measures accuracy, before you compare price.

Most COI tracking software demos look alike, and most lists of COI tracking software features read alike too. Someone uploads a clean certificate, the fields fill in, a green check appears, and an expiration reminder gets scheduled. The differences that matter on a construction project don't show up until a contractor's endorsement is wrong, a project carries its own limits, or a policy lapses halfway through the job.

This COI tracking software checklist is for general contractors' risk, compliance and project teams writing down what they need before they shortlist tools. It names no vendors. It lists 12 points, ranks the COI tracking software features by how much they matter, and gives a test you can run with your own documents.

The order is the weighting. Points 1 to 5 decide whether a gap gets caught at all, so they count most. Points 6 to 9 decide how fast it gets fixed and who's accountable. Points 10 to 12 decide whether the tool fits your systems, your security review and your budget.

Forsured makes COI tracking software, so read the checklist knowing that. It's written to be useful whichever tool you pick, and the tests work the same on ours as on anyone's.

What should a general contractor look for in COI tracking software?

A general contractor should look for COI tracking software that holds requirements by project, reads endorsements instead of checkboxes, sends gaps back to the broker, tracks renewals across every project a contractor works on, and makes clear who approves each contractor COI. COI tracking software features like integrations, security and price come after those, because a tool that misses a gap is expensive at any price.

What is on the COI tracking software checklist?

The COI tracking software checklist below has 12 points. The test column is what to bring or ask in the demo.

COI tracking software checklist: 12 points and how to test each one
#Look forHow to test it
1Requirements held by project and by tradeLoad two projects with different umbrella limits and check one contractor against both
2Where each requirement came fromAsk to see the contract section a requirement points back to
3Endorsement review, not checkbox readingUpload a certificate with the additional insured box checked and no endorsement
4Ongoing and completed operations checked separatelySend an ongoing operations form with no completed operations form
5Each failure explained, missing documents treated as failsLeave out the waiver of subrogation and see how the result reads
6The broker in the fixAsk who gets the deficiency request and whether it quotes the requirement
7Renewals and lapses tracked by policyAsk what happens on the expiration date if no renewal has come in
8Wrap-ups and blanket policiesAsk how an OCIP or CCIP enrollment changes what a contractor must show
9Who makes the final callAsk what's automated, what a person reviews and how accuracy is tested
10Fit with your project toolsAsk what syncs with your project and accounting systems, in which direction
11Security and document accessAsk for the SOC report and who can see each document
12Price in writingAsk for year-one and year-two totals at your contractor count

Which COI tracking software features matter most?

The COI tracking software features that matter most are the first five on the list, because they decide whether a gap is caught before a trade is on site. Here's what to look for in each group.

Project requirements (points 1 and 2)

Project requirements change from job to job. One owner wants $10 million in umbrella limits, another wants $5 million, and a public project adds its own forms. A tool that keeps one set of requirements per contractor will pass a certificate that fails the project it's for. Look for project requirements set by project and by trade tier, with each line traced back to the contract section it came from. Our state COI requirements pages show how much the rules vary before an owner adds anything.

Endorsement review (points 3 to 5)

Endorsement review is where most gaps hide. An additional insured is someone not automatically insured under a policy, so the endorsement, not the checkbox, is what extends coverage to you. Good endorsement review reads the form itself, checks ongoing operations and completed operations as separate items, and treats primary and noncontributory, waiver of subrogation and per project aggregate as their own lines. When something fails, the result should say what's missing and what the project needs. Our guide to endorsement review in COI tracking software goes deeper on what to expect.

Fixing gaps and keeping every contractor COI current (points 6 to 8)

A gap is only half found until the contractor's broker fixes it. Look for a tool that sends the deficiency request to the broker with the requirement quoted, takes the corrected document back and re-checks it, and keeps an audit trail of each round. Then look at time. A contractor COI that passed in March can lapse in July, so the tool should track each policy across every project that contractor works on, ask for renewals with endorsements before expiration, and treat no renewal on the expiration date as a lapse. If you run wrap-ups, ask how an OCIP or CCIP changes what each enrolled contractor must show.

Who decides, fit, security and price (points 9 to 12)

Two COI tracking software features are easy to skip in a demo: who decides, and how the tool fits your systems. Ask the vendor to say plainly what's automated and what a person reviews. The NAIC model bulletin on AI systems asks insurers to govern how they use AI, and the same questions fit a COI tool: how it's tested, how errors are caught and who signs off on an approval or a waiver. For fit, check what syncs with your project tools, and look for a current listing in the Procore Marketplace if you run Procore. For security, ask for the vendor's SOC report and use our vendor security questions. For price, get it in writing at your contractor count, and compare it with what COI tracking software costs on published price lists.

How do you use the checklist in a demo?

Use the COI tracking software checklist as a score sheet. Mark each of the 12 points pass, partial or fail for every vendor, weight points 1 to 5 most heavily, and run the tests with your own documents rather than the vendor's sample.

  1. Pick one active project and pull its insurance requirements.
  2. Bring three documents: a certificate with the additional insured box checked and no endorsement, a contractor COI with an umbrella below the project limit, and a renewal that's due soon.
  3. Ask the vendor to load the project requirements and review the documents live.
  4. Watch what happens to each failure: how it's explained, who gets the fix request, and when the item clears.
  5. Ask the questions in points 9 to 12 and get the answers in writing.

Our COI tracking software demo questions give you the exact wording to use, and our COI Journal report on what to require from any COI tool turns this checklist into a 20-line specification for a formal evaluation. When you're ready to compare tools, start with the best COI tracking software for construction.

You've been asked to price COI tracking software, and most vendor sites send you to a demo before they show a number. That makes it hard to set a budget, or to tell whether a quote is fair. COI tracking software cost depends on how many contractors you track, how much of the review the vendor's team does, and a few charges that show up late.

This guide is for general contractors' risk, compliance and finance teams putting a number on construction COI tracking, and for anyone comparing a quote they already have. COI tracking software cost for construction starts at free and runs to $10,000 a year or more. Paid self-service software starts around $500 a year at Billy, $11.40 per vendor a year at bcs and about $300 a month at PINS Advantage. Managed tiers carry annual minimums of $7,500 to $10,000.

Is free COI tracking software enough for a general contractor?

The question that separates them is how far each one reads: does it name the endorsement type, flag a missing required form, read the wording against your project requirements, or read the full policy? That matters because the certificate is only a summary. Six of the eight tools are listed on the Procore Marketplace, and they do different things with the connection. For Procore COI tracking, ask where the status lands and whether it can hold a payment:

  • bcs connects to Procore alongside Yardi and MRI.
  • Forsured offers a Procore integration to early access customers, outside the Marketplace for now.
  • Certificial doesn't list a Procore integration.

Procore COI tracking only helps if the review behind it is right. A green status in Procore built on an unread endorsement is still a gap.

AI COI tracking: who makes the final call

Every tool here uses AI to read certificates. The real question with AI COI tracking is what happens after the AI reads it:

  • AI decides: illumend's Lumie makes each decision and only escalates items it can't resolve.
  • AI with a check: bcs reads each certificate twice and sends disagreements to a person. TrustLayer's endorsement review is confirmed by a person.
  • Your team decides: Forsured and PINS Advantage find and explain each issue, and your people approve, reject or waive it. Certificial extracts endorsement details for you to accept or reject.
  • Someone else's team decides: Billy's managed plan, bcs full service, Jones's specialists and TrustLayer+ put their reviewers on your certificates.

Pick the model that matches who carries the risk at your company when a claim lands. For the endorsements that most often decide that claim, see whether additional insured status covers you after the job is done and what primary and noncontributory means on a COI.

The best COI tracking software for one general contractor can be the wrong fit for the next. Before you book demos, answer these five questions about your own subcontractor COI tracking, and use the answers to narrow the list of COI tracking software for construction you'll see:

  2. Who reads the endorsements today? If nobody does, put endorsement review ahead of everything else on your list.
  3. How does a gap get fixed? Watch a demo of a deficient COI going to a broker and coming back corrected.
  4. Where do your teams work? If it's Procore, ask what Procore COI tracking status the tool writes back and whether it can hold payment.
  5. Software or service? Decide whether your team will review AI COI tracking results, or whether you'd rather pay someone to handle subcontractor COI tracking for you.

State rules matter too. Workers' comp thresholds and anti-indemnity statutes change what you can require, so check contractor insurance requirements by state before you build your templates.

item.title: Contractor backlog fell to 8.1 months. What it means for COIs
item.description: ABC's Construction Backlog Indicator dropped 0.6 months to 8.1 in October 2026. What the numbers say, and why thinner backlogs matter for contractor COIs.
item.content:encoded:
• ABC's Construction Backlog Indicator fell to 8.1 months in October 2026, down 0.6 months from September and 0.3 months from a year earlier.
  • The drop came from contractors without data center work. Their backlog fell from 8.3 to 7.6 months, while contractors with data center work rose from 11.3 to 11.5 months.
  • Infrastructure backlog fell to 8.7 months, its lowest since May 2025. Profit margin expectations improved, but sales and staffing expectations fell.
  • When backlog thins, more contractors bid on work outside their usual size or scope. Check that each contractor COI meets this project's requirements, not the contractor's last job's.

Contractor backlog fell sharply in October. Associated Builders and Contractors reported Nov. 10 that its Construction Backlog Indicator dropped to 8.1 months, down 0.6 months from September and 0.3 months from October 2025. For owners and GCs, a thinner pipeline means more contractors chasing each job, and that's worth a closer look at the COIs that come with the bids.

What ABC reported

"Backlog fell sharply in October, returning to levels not consistently observed since last winter," said ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu.

The split behind the number is stark:

GroupSeptemberOctober
All contractors8.7 months8.1 months
Contractors without data center work (88%)8.3 months7.6 months
Contractors with data center work11.3 months11.5 months

ABC notes that most contractors doing data center work have more than $100 million in annual revenue. By category, infrastructure backlog fell to 8.7 months, the lowest since May 2025, while heavy industrial backlog rose to a 15-month high.

The Construction Confidence Index was mixed. Profit margin expectations improved, while sales and staffing expectations fell. All three readings stayed above 50, the level ABC says signals expected growth over the next six months. Even so, Basu noted that "roughly 1 in 4 contractors still expect their margins to shrink over the next six months," citing recent increases in materials prices and borrowing costs.

Why it matters for contractor COIs

When backlog shrinks, contractors widen their search for work. That can mean bidding on projects larger than their usual jobs, in a new sector, or in a new state.

Their insurance was usually bought for the work they normally do. A program that fit a $10 million job can fall short on a $50 million one:

  • Limits. Umbrella and excess limits may sit below what a larger project requires.
  • Aggregates. A general aggregate shared across more jobs runs thinner. A per project aggregate keeps yours separate.
  • Endorsements. Additional insured, completed operations and waiver wording may not match the new project's contract.

None of that shows up in a backlog number. It shows up when you read each contractor COI against the project requirements for the job in front of you, not the contractor's last one.

Forsured checks every contractor COI against your project requirements and flags the gaps, so a competitive bid market doesn't bring a coverage gap with it.

Which leads to the question that matters on every job, whatever the backlog: how do you check a contractor COI against your project requirements?

item.title: What does per project aggregate mean on a contractor COI?
item.description: A contractor's general aggregate is shared by every job it works. The per project aggregate endorsement, CG 25 03, gives your project its own. What to check.
item.content:encoded:
• Per project aggregate means the contractor's general aggregate limit applies separately to each designated construction project, instead of one limit shared by all of its work.
  • Without it, claims paid on the contractor's other jobs during the policy year reduce the same aggregate that's supposed to protect your project.
  • ISO's standard form is CG 25 03. It covers ongoing operations at the scheduled projects and doesn't change the products-completed operations aggregate.
  • On the ACORD 25, look for the PRO-JECT box under GEN'L AGGREGATE LIMIT APPLIES PER, then ask for the endorsement and check its schedule names your project.

Per project aggregate means the contractor's general liability aggregate applies separately to your project. Without it, one general aggregate limit covers every job the contractor works during the policy year, and claims on those other jobs use up the same limit your project is counting on.

What is the general aggregate?

A general liability policy has two kinds of limits. The each occurrence limit caps what it pays for any one occurrence. The general aggregate caps the total for the policy year.

IRMI defines the general aggregate as "the maximum limit of insurance payable during any given annual policy period" for covered losses other than specified exposures. Products-completed operations claims "are paid out of a separate aggregate." Once paid losses reach the general aggregate, the limit is exhausted.

That's the catch for an owner or GC. A contractor COI showing a $2 million general aggregate tells you what the contractor bought, not how much of it is left. The ACORD 25 says so in its own fine print: "LIMITS SHOWN MAY HAVE BEEN REDUCED BY PAID CLAIMS." A busy contractor with a bad year on two other jobs can show up to yours with far less.

What does CG 25 03 change?

The ISO endorsement CG 25 03, Designated Construction Project(s) General Aggregate Limit, fixes that. IRMI says it makes the general aggregate "apply separately to each designated construction project," which lets a contractor meet contract requirements for a specified amount of insurance on a specific project. Insureon puts it more simply: it "gives each construction project its own aggregate limit."

The form itself, in the CG 25 03 05 09 edition published by the New York State Office of General Services, spells out how it works:

  • Each project gets its own limit. "A separate Designated Construction Project General Aggregate Limit applies to each designated construction project," equal to the general aggregate shown in the declarations.
  • Your claims don't touch the policy aggregate. Payments on your project reduce your project's limit, and "Such payments shall not reduce the General Aggregate Limit shown in the Declarations."
  • The each occurrence limit still applies. The other limits continue to apply, subject to the project's aggregate.
  • A delayed project is still the same project. A project that's abandoned, delayed or restarted is still deemed the same construction project.

Insureon works through an example. A contractor with a $2 million general aggregate has claims of $1.5 million, $400,000 and $1 million on three different projects in one policy year. Without the endorsement, those claims total $2.9 million against a $2 million general aggregate. With a per project aggregate, each claim draws on its own project's limit, and Insureon says all three would be covered. The per occurrence limit still applies to each one.

Which aggregate does each claim reduce?

CG 25 03 sorts every claim into one of three buckets:

Which aggregate a claim reduces under CG 25 03, per the CG 25 03 05 09 form
ClaimAggregate it reducesAggregates it doesn't reduce
Ongoing operations at a project in the scheduleThat project's designated aggregateThe policy's general aggregate and other projects' limits
Anything not tied only to a scheduled projectThe general aggregate or products-completed operations aggregateAny designated project aggregate
Products-completed operationsThe products-completed operations aggregateThe general aggregate and every designated project aggregate

Does a per project aggregate cover products-completed operations?

No, and the third row is the one GCs miss. CG 25 03 doesn't separate completed operations. IRMI confirms the endorsement "does not affect the policy's other limits, including the products-completed operations aggregate limit," and notes a separate designated project products-completed operations aggregate endorsement can make a similar change. If your project requirements call for a per project completed operations aggregate too, ask for that endorsement by name, and read completed operations additional insured coverage for the rest of the after-the-job picture.

How does a contractor COI show a per project aggregate?

The ACORD 25 has a field labeled "GEN'L AGGREGATE LIMIT APPLIES PER," with three boxes: POLICY, PRO-JECT and LOC. A checked PRO-JECT box is the certificate's summary of a per project aggregate. POLICY means one general aggregate for everything. LOC points to a per location aggregate, the related CG 25 04 form that Insureon describes for businesses with several locations.

Like every box on the certificate, PRO-JECT is a summary. The endorsement does the work, and its schedule decides which projects get their own limit. The CG 25 03 schedule is a blank list headed "Designated Construction Project(s)," with any missing details shown in the declarations. If your project isn't in that list, your claims fall into the second row of the table and share the general aggregate with everything else.

What does a per project aggregate cost?

Usually little. Insureon says a per project aggregate endorsement "can typically be added for a nominal cost," and that there's no legal requirement to carry one. Contractors add it to meet contract terms set by clients, general contractors, lenders or bonding companies. That makes it a fair ask in your project requirements, and an easy one for a contractor's broker to say yes to.

How do you check a per project aggregate on a contractor COI?

  1. Confirm your project requirements call for a per project aggregate, and at what amount.
  2. Look for the PRO-JECT box on the contractor COI, then ask for the CG 25 03 endorsement or the insurer's equivalent.
  3. Check the schedule. It should name your project, or the declarations should.
  4. Check the PRODUCTS - COMP/OP AGG amount on its own. CG 25 03 doesn't separate it.
  5. Check the related endorsements in the same pass: additional insured status, primary and noncontributory wording and the waiver of subrogation.
  6. Recheck at renewal, when a new policy year brings a new schedule.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against your project requirements, including the per project aggregate endorsement behind the limits shown, for the life of the job. For the full field-by-field review, see how to read a certificate of insurance, or run a free COI risk check on one project.

item.title: Insurance compliance is on the trades tech map. It's filed under getting paid.
item.description: Suffolk Technologies' new trades tech map puts insurance compliance under getting paid. Why it belongs at the start of the job, and why compliance isn't coverage.
item.content:encoded:
• Suffolk Technologies' November 2026 map groups emerging tools for trade contractors into five stages: win and staff work, run the business, plan and coordinate work, do the work, and get paid and manage cash.
  • Insurance compliance is on it, filed under payment compliance in the get paid stage, next to pay apps and lien waivers.
  • That placement matches how much of the industry runs it: as a gate on payment. By the time a payment is held, the crew has already been working with the gap.
  • Two shifts would make it a real operational gain: check coverage when a contractor is staffed onto the job and keep checking during the work, and test the coverage itself against the project requirements, not just the certificate's boxes.

Suffolk Technologies just published one of the more useful pieces of construction tech writing this year: A Better Tech Stack for the Trades. Its market map sorts the tools built for trade contractors into five stages of the job. Insurance compliance is on it, in the last column, under getting paid. We think that's an honest picture of how the industry runs compliance today, and a clear sign of where the next gain is.

What Suffolk Technologies mapped

The piece starts with the labor problem. Suffolk Technologies cites estimates of a skilled-labor gap of up to 600,000 U.S. workers, and notes that for every five people leaving the industry, only two enter it. Its answer is technology "designed around the way work actually happens" in the field.

The map, titled "Enabling the next phase of jobsite execution," follows a trade contractor through five stages:

StageWhat it covers
Win and staff workBidding and estimating, recruiting and training, safety and onboarding
Run the businessHR, payroll and crews, accounting, sales, financial intelligence
Plan and coordinate workProject intelligence, field collaboration, materials and procurement
Do the workField tools and diagnostics, automation and robotics
Get paid and manage cashPay apps and billing, payment compliance, working capital

Two arguments stand out. First, tech sprawl is real. The article says "the explosion of back-office tools is unmanageable in the long run." Second, the payoff is structural: modern tools let firms "move away from linear revenue to headcount growth." That's the right frame. The goal isn't more software. It's more work done per person, with less friction.

Where insurance compliance landed

On the map, tools for tracking certificates and prequalifying contractors sit in the payment compliance box, next to lien waivers and draw management. In other words, compliance is grouped with the paperwork that releases money.

That's accurate. On a lot of projects, the moment anyone looks hard at a contractor COI is when a payment is about to go out. If the certificate has lapsed or a requirement is missing, the payment waits until it's fixed.

The problem is timing. By the time a payment is held, the crew has already been on site, sometimes for weeks, working with the gap. If someone was hurt or something was damaged in that window, holding the check doesn't change who pays for the claim.

Move it to the start of the job

The map's first stage, win and staff work, already includes safety and onboarding. That's where insurance compliance belongs too. A contractor should prove its insurance meets the project requirements when it's staffed onto the job, before it mobilizes, the same way crews complete orientation before they start.

Watch: Insurance compliance is the elephant on every jobsite (0:30). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

Then it should keep running in the do the work stage. Policies renew, change and cancel mid-project. A check that happens once at onboarding and again at each pay app misses everything in between.

Placed that way, payment becomes a confirmation, not a discovery. The pay app goes out on time because compliance was already clean.

From compliance to coverage

The second shift matters more. Most compliance work today confirms the paperwork matches a checklist: a certificate is on file, the additional insured box is checked, the limits are listed. As we've written before, compliance isn't coverage. A certificate can check every box and still leave the project exposed.

Coverage questions live in the policies and endorsements, not on the certificate:

  • Does the additional insured endorsement cover completed operations, or only ongoing work?
  • Is the coverage primary and noncontributory, as the project requirements say?
  • Is waiver of subrogation actually endorsed, or just typed on the form?
  • Do the umbrella limits sit over the right underlying policies?

Those answers decide who pays when something goes wrong. They're also the slowest part of the job to check by hand, which is exactly the kind of back-office work the article says the trades need to shed.

The bigger point

Suffolk Technologies is right that the trades deserve a better tech stack, built around the field. Its map already shows that insurance compliance is part of that stack. The next step is moving it from the end of the job to the start, and from checking paperwork to checking coverage.

That's the layer we're building at Forsured. If you want to see what it looks like on your own paperwork, send us one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two at hello@forsured.ai, and we'll run a free check.
