item.title: Does additional insured status cover you after the job is done? Completed operations, CG 20 10 and CG 20 37
item.description: Completed operations additional insured coverage explained: why CG 20 10 stops at completion, what CG 20 37 adds, and what to check on a contractor COI.
item.content:encoded:
• CG 20 10 covered finished work until its 1993 edition. Every edition since covers only ongoing operations.
  • CG 20 37 exists only to add additional insured status for completed operations. It doesn't cover the work in progress.
  • The 2013 editions cap both forms at what your contract requires, so the contract wording now matters as much as the form.
  • Check the products and completed operations aggregate on the certificate, and keep collecting certificates after turnover.

A checked additional insured box on a contractor COI usually means CG 20 10, and CG 20 10 stops covering you the day the work is done. The claims a GC or owner worries about most often show up later: a roof that leaks after turnover, a stair that fails a year in. Covering those takes completed operations coverage, and that takes its own endorsement.

Why does CG 20 10 stop covering you at completion?

CG 20 10 stops at completion because ISO rewrote it in 1993. The original 1985 edition, CG 20 10 11 85, covered liability arising out of the contractor's "your work," which included both ongoing and completed operations. Construction Executive explains that the October 1993 edition changed the wording to liability arising out of "your ongoing operations," which effectively removed additional insured status for completed operations.

Watch: What does additional insured mean? The sixth-grade version (0:33). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

Insurance Journal puts it in one line: "'Ongoing operations' does not include completed operations." Every edition of CG 20 10 since 1993 works the same way.

What counts as completed operations?

Completed operations is the contractor's work once it's finished. IRMI defines it as work that has been completed as the contract calls for, work finished at one site of a multi-site contract, or work that has been put to its intended use.

The trigger is when the injury or damage happens, not when the work was done. The County of Sonoma's insurance guide makes the same point: CG 20 10 doesn't cover injury or damage after the work is done, which is a completed operations hazard that needs a separate endorsement.

What does CG 20 37 add?

CG 20 37 adds additional insured status for completed operations, and nothing else. ISO released it in October 2001, and Construction Executive describes its sole purpose as bringing back the ability to add an additional insured to completed operations coverage. Insurance Journal notes it doesn't cover ongoing operations.

So the two forms split the job in time, and the editions have narrowed along the way:

CG 20 10 and CG 20 37 editions and what each covers
EditionCovers you forWhat changed
CG 20 10 11 85Ongoing and completed operationsOriginal "your work" wording
CG 20 10 10 93Ongoing operations only"Your ongoing operations" replaced "your work"
CG 20 37 10 01Completed operations onlyNew form to restore completed operations
CG 20 10 and CG 20 37 07 04Same split"Caused, in whole or in part, by" replaced "arising out of"
CG 20 10 and CG 20 37 04 13Same splitLimited to what the law permits, what the contract requires, and the lower of the contract limit or policy limit

The 2004 change narrowed coverage to liability the contractor's acts or omissions caused, in whole or in part. The 2013 change ties coverage to your contract, so a vague insurance clause now gets you only what it clearly asks for.

Does a blanket endorsement cover completed operations?

A blanket additional insured endorsement covers completed operations only if its wording says so. Forms like CG 20 38 and CG 20 33 add additional insureds automatically when a written contract requires it, which saves scheduling every owner and GC by name. But whether completed operations is included depends on the form and its edition. See per written contract additional insured for how those forms differ.

Watch for insurer-specific forms too. Sonoma County won't accept a proprietary completed operations endorsement that limits coverage to the current policy period, because a claim about finished work can arrive after that policy has renewed.

How do you check completed operations on a contractor COI?

You check completed operations on a contractor COI by looking past the certificate to the endorsements and the limits:

  1. Confirm your project requirements call for additional insured status for both ongoing and completed operations, and say for how long after completion.
  2. Ask for both endorsements behind the checked ADDL INSD box, or a blanket form that names completed operations. Note each form number and edition.
  3. Check the "products - comp/op agg" limit on the ACORD 25. That's the aggregate completed operations claims draw from, and it should meet your requirement.
  4. Check that additional insured coverage is primary where your contract requires it, with primary and noncontributory wording, and that a waiver of subrogation is attached.
  5. Keep collecting certificates and endorsements after turnover for as long as completed operations coverage must last.

Forsured reads the endorsement forms attached to each contractor COI and flags an additional insured endorsement that covers ongoing operations but not completed operations, against the requirements set for that project.

What do public owners require for completed operations?

Public owners often spell out completed operations by form number, which makes their requirements a useful model for your own. The County of Sonoma, for example, requires both CG 20 10 04 13 and CG 20 37 04 13 for work performed for the County. So a contractor working for the County needs additional insured status for ongoing operations and for completed operations, not one or the other.

The County also says it isn't limited to ISO forms and will accept equivalent language. That's a practical standard for a GC too. What matters is what the endorsement covers, not whose name is printed at the bottom of it. If a contractor COI points to an insurer's own form, read it the same way you'd read CG 20 37: who it covers, for which operations, and for how long after completion.

If you write project requirements for a public job, start from the owner's insurance section and copy its form numbers and editions into your contractor requirements word for word. Your contractors' coverage then matches what the owner expects from you.

What else affects completed operations claims?

Two other details decide how much a completed operations claim can pay. The first is the aggregate: a general aggregate shared across every job the contractor works can be spent before your claim arrives, so ask for a per project aggregate. The second is state law. Anti-indemnity statutes in some states limit what additional insured requirements can ask for, so check the contractor COI requirements for your state.

item.title: Will a COI give you notice of cancellation if a contractor's policy lapses mid-project?
item.description: Notice of cancellation on the ACORD 25 doesn't promise to tell you a contractor's policy ended. What the box says, what a lapse costs a GC, and how to get notice.
item.content:encoded:
• Usually not. Since the 2009/09 edition, the ACORD 25 cancellation box says only that notice "will be delivered in accordance with the policy provisions."
  • Standard policy provisions send cancellation notice to the named insured, the contractor, not to the certificate holder.
  • A lapse mid-project can land on the GC. In Minnesota, a GC is liable for workers' compensation benefits when a contractor it hired is uninsured.
  • New York's certificate law bars requiring certificate terms the policy doesn't contain, so typing notice wording onto the certificate doesn't create it.
  • To hear about a cancellation, ask for an insurer endorsement that schedules you, track every expiration date, and keep checking coverage for the life of the job.

Usually not. The notice of cancellation box on the standard ACORD 25 certificate reads like a promise, but since the 2009/09 edition it only points back to the policy. And the policy usually sends cancellation notice to the contractor who bought it, not to you. So when a contractor's coverage lapses in the middle of your project, the certificate in your file keeps saying everything is fine.

What does the notice of cancellation box say?

Here is the wording on the current ACORD 25, the 2025/12 edition:

Should any of the above described policies be cancelled before the expiration date thereof, notice will be delivered in accordance with the policy provisions.

Older editions talked about mailing the certificate holder written notice within a stated number of days, though with a line saying that failing to do so imposed no obligation on the insurer or agent. The 2009/09 change dropped the days and handed the notice of cancellation question to the policy.

So the real question is what the policy says. Standard cancellation conditions run between the insurer and its named insured. Unless an endorsement adds you, the owner or GC on the certificate isn't on that list.

Why can't the certificate fix it?

It's tempting to ask the agent to type a note into the ACORD 25 description box, such as "30 days' notice to the certificate holder." That doesn't create the right.

Watch: What is a certificate of insurance (COI)? Basically a selfie (0:32). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

New York put this in statute. Insurance Law section 502 says a certificate "shall not amend, extend, or alter the coverage" of the policy it refers to, and "shall further not confer to any person any rights beyond those expressly provided by the policy." It also bars anyone from willfully requiring certificate language the policy "does not expressly include." New York's Department of Financial Services traces the rules to a new Article 5 of the Insurance Law, added by laws passed in 2014 and 2015.

The certificate summarizes. The policy decides.

What happens if a contractor's workers' compensation or liability coverage lapses mid-project?

A lapse doesn't announce itself. The ACORD 25 contractor COI in your file still shows the old POLICY EFF and POLICY EXP dates. If the policy was canceled for nonpayment last month, nothing on that certificate changes. You find out when you check again, or when a claim comes in.

By then the cost can land on you. Workers' compensation is the clearest case, because some states, Minnesota among them, make the GC answer for a hired contractor's missing workers' compensation coverage. The Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry explains that when a contractor a GC hires fails to carry workers' compensation, the general contractor or an intermediate contractor is liable for the benefits due that contractor's injured employees, and benefits "may be collected from any contractor up the chain." That's Minnesota Statutes section 176.215. Other states have their own rules, so check yours on the contractor COI requirements for your state.

Construction Executive makes the same point more broadly: if a contractor fails to enroll an employee in workers' compensation, "immunity can be lost," and the GC can be held liable for uncovered workers. A lapse on general liability creates a different gap. Claims from that contractor's work may have no policy to respond, and Amwins notes that when a contractor's insurance is insufficient, "the GC may be pulled into the claim."

How can you hear about a cancellation in time?

Here are the ways to learn a contractor's policy ended, and what each one catches:

Ways to learn a contractor's policy was canceled or lapsed
MethodWhat it catchesWhat it misses
The ACORD 25 cancellation boxNothing on its own; it points to the policyAny notice the policy doesn't send you
An insurer endorsement that schedules youCancellation, with written notice for the days set in its schedulePolicies without the endorsement
A renewal certificate before each POLICY EXP datePolicies that expire without renewalCancellation before the expiration date
Ongoing verification of each contractor COICancellations and expirations, for the life of the jobNothing, if it runs on every policy your requirements list

Watch: Check your contractor's insurance every job, even the ones you trust (0:37). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

Ask for a notice of cancellation endorsement. The fix is an insurer endorsement that schedules you to receive notice. BCS's example: "we agree to mail prior written notice of cancellation to the person(s) or organization(s) shown in the Schedule." Another sample BCS quotes gives at least 60 days' written notice of cancellation, or at least 10 days in the case of nonpayment of premium. BCS also warned these endorsements "are not generally available and are used sparingly by Insurers," so ask early.

Track every policy period. Note each policy's POLICY EXP date, including workers' compensation, from the contractor COI and ask for a renewal certificate before that date, not after.

Keep checking for the life of the job. A COI is a snapshot from the day it was issued. Put the check in your project requirements and repeat it, so a lapse shows up before a loss does.

What should your project requirements say about cancellation?

Write the notice of cancellation and the follow-through into the contract, so you aren't relying on the certificate:

  1. Require the contractor to keep every listed policy in force for the life of the job, and for completed operations, for the period after completion your contract sets.
  2. Require a notice of cancellation endorsement scheduling you where the insurer offers one, and require the contractor to tell you directly if any policy is canceled or not renewed.
  3. Require renewal certificates and endorsements before each POLICY EXP date.
  4. Pass the same requirements down to every lower-tier contractor. Construction Executive calls this "an unbroken vertical chain of contractual requirements to obtain and maintain proper insurance."
  5. Keep the records. Amwins recommends collecting and retaining certificates for at least 5 to 8 years.

Coverage that ends quietly is the gap a file of PDFs can't show. Check the endorsements behind the rest of the certificate the same way, starting with completed operations and the per project aggregate.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against your project requirements and keeps checking for the life of the job, so a canceled or expired policy doesn't hide in a file of old PDFs. item.title: What does waiver of subrogation mean on a contractor COI?
item.description: A waiver of subrogation stops a contractor's insurer from suing you to recover what it paid. What it means, how WC 00 03 13 works, and what to check on each COI.
item.content:encoded:
• A waiver of subrogation is the insurer's acknowledgment that it has no right to recover what it paid from a liable third party, such as the owner or GC.
  • Insurers agree to it because their insured already gave up its own right of recovery in a contract. Policies generally allow that before a loss, not after.
  • The SUBR WVD box on the ACORD 25 is a summary. The waiver comes from the policy wording or an endorsement.
  • The workers' comp form, NCCI's WC 00 03 13, applies only to parties named in its schedule, and a premium charge may apply.

A waiver of subrogation is an insurer's agreement not to go after a third party to recover what it paid on a claim. On a construction project, that third party is usually you: the owner or GC. Without the waiver, a contractor's insurer that pays for a loss could turn around and sue you to get its money back, even though the contractor promised in its contract not to.

What is subrogation?

When an insurer pays a claim, it can step into its insured's shoes and pursue whoever caused the loss. That's subrogation. In standard commercial policies, IRMI notes, the right sits in a condition called "Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others to Us." The workers' comp policy says it directly: "We have a right to recover our payments from anyone liable for an injury covered by this policy."

IRMI defines a waiver of subrogation as "an acknowledgment by an insurer that it has no right to subrogate against a liable third party." It gives up that recovery right against named parties, or against anyone a contract requires.

Why do construction contracts require a waiver of subrogation?

Because the contract has already asked the contractor to give up its own right of recovery against the owner and GC. IRMI explains that insurers usually agree to a waiver of subrogation as a response to the insured having waived its own right of recovery against a third party. The insurer's waiver is the proof that the contract promise holds, and that it didn't cost the contractor its coverage.

Timing matters. IRMI says policies generally don't bar coverage if an insured waives its right of recovery before a loss. But coverage is excluded from many policies if subrogation is waived after a loss, because that would violate the principle of indemnity. So the signed contract has to come first, before the contractor starts work.

Where does a waiver of subrogation come from?

Like additional insured status, a waiver of subrogation comes from policy wording, not from the certificate. Here's where it shows up, and what each piece proves:

Where a waiver of subrogation appears and what each piece proves
WhereWhat it saysWhat it proves
Your contractThe contractor waives its own right to recover from youThe contractor's promise, which must come before a loss
The policy endorsement, such as WC 00 03 13The insurer won't enforce its recovery right against scheduled partiesThe waiver itself
The SUBR WVD box on the ACORD 25A check markA summary only; certain policies may require an endorsement

The ACORD 25 says so in its IMPORTANT box: "If SUBROGATION IS WAIVED, subject to the terms and conditions of the policy, certain policies may require an endorsement." It adds that a statement on the certificate doesn't confer rights to the certificate holder in place of that endorsement. A checked SUBR WVD box on a contractor COI is where your review starts, not where it ends.

How does WC 00 03 13 work?

On workers' compensation, the standard form is NCCI's WC 00 03 13, "Waiver of Our Right to Recover From Others Endorsement." NCRB's instruction sheet describes it as used to waive the company's right of subrogation against named third parties. Its key line: "We will not enforce our right against the person or organization named in the Schedule." Three details matter:

  • It's limited to the Schedule. The form says it "shall not operate directly or indirectly to benefit anyone not named in the Schedule."
  • It can be tied to a written contract. An optional sentence limits it to work done "under a written contract that requires you to obtain this agreement from us."
  • Residual market policies get a blanket waiver only. NCRB's instructions say that for those policies, only a blanket waiver may be applied.

General liability, auto and umbrella policies each carry their own waiver of subrogation wording, often by endorsement. Ask for each one your project requirements list, and read it the same way: who it covers, and whether it depends on a written contract.

Does a waiver of subrogation cost extra?

It can. NCRB's instructions say a premium charge may apply for the endorsement on both voluntary and assigned risk policies. Tennessee's insurance department, for example, allows a carrier-set charge in the voluntary market, based on the carrier's evaluation of the exposure. For assigned risk policies, the charge is 5% of the manual premium for the work the waiver covers, with a $250 minimum per waiver. That's one reason a contractor may resist adding the waiver of subrogation until a contract requires it.

What should you ask the contractor's broker for?

When a contractor COI comes in with the SUBR WVD box checked, send one short request back to the contractor's broker. Ask for a copy of each waiver endorsement, with its form number and edition, for every policy marked SUBR WVD. For workers' comp, that's usually WC 00 03 13. Ask whether the schedule names you or uses the blanket written contract wording, and whether the waiver reaches every party your project requirements list, such as the owner and lender. If a policy has no waiver endorsement, ask the broker to add one before work starts. A waiver added after a loss may not help.

If the broker sends back a WC 00 03 13 with a blank schedule, the form names no one, and it doesn't benefit anyone not named in the Schedule. Ask the broker to fill it in.

How do you check a waiver of subrogation on a contractor COI?

  1. Confirm your project requirements call for a waiver of subrogation, and on which policies: general liability, auto, workers' comp, umbrella.
  2. Ask for the endorsement behind each checked SUBR WVD box on the contractor COI. Note the form number and edition.
  3. Check that it names you, or applies to anyone a written contract requires, and that the contract is signed before work starts.
  4. Check the related endorsements in the same pass: additional insured status, primary and noncontributory wording and completed operations coverage.
  5. Recheck at renewal, when endorsements can drop off.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, including the waiver of subrogation endorsements behind the checkboxes, for the life of the job. item.title: Is U.S. construction spending down? What the September 2026 numbers show
item.description: Census data released Nov 2 shows U.S. construction spending fell 1.9% in September 2026. Residential pulled it down while nonresidential grew.
item.content:encoded:
• Yes. U.S. construction spending ran at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $2,186.1 billion in September 2026, down 1.9% from August and 2.7% from a year earlier, the Census Bureau reported Nov 2.
  • Spending for the first nine months of 2026 was $1,649.6 billion, 2.9% below the same period in 2025.
  • Residential drove the drop: private residential spending fell 5.5% in the month.
  • Nonresidential kept growing. Private nonresidential rose 1.1% from August, and total nonresidential was 1.8% above September 2025.

Yes. U.S. construction spending fell 1.9% in September 2026, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $2,186.1 billion, the Census Bureau reported Monday. That's 2.7% below September 2025. For the first nine months of the year, spending totaled $1,649.6 billion, down 2.9% from the same stretch of 2025.

The headline hides a split, though. Almost all of the decline is residential.

Where the drop came from

SegmentSeptember 2026 (annual rate)vs. Augustvs. Sept. 2025
Total$2,186.1B-1.9%-2.7%
Total residential$861.2B-5.4%-8.8%
Private nonresidential$790.6B+1.1%+2.3%
Total nonresidential$1,325.0B+0.6%+1.8%
Public$546.8B-0.1%+1.0%

Private residential alone fell 5.5% in the month, to $848.8 billion. Nonresidential, the work most commercial GCs and trade contractors depend on, is the part still growing.

On the public side, spending was essentially flat. Educational spending was $113.1 billion, virtually unchanged, and highway spending was $149.2 billion, down 0.3%.

These are preliminary numbers. Census revises each month, and August was revised in this release. The next update is due Dec 1.

What it means for project requirements

A softer overall market tends to mean tighter bids and more competition for nonresidential work. That can bring new names onto your jobs: trade contractors you haven't worked with before, bidding into a segment that's still growing.

New relationships are where insurance gaps hide. Before a new contractor mobilizes:

  1. Check its COI against your project requirements, line by line, not just for a valid policy.
  2. Ask for the additional insured and primary and noncontributory endorsements, not just the certificate.
  3. Track expiration dates from day one, so coverage doesn't lapse mid-project.

For each new contractor, the question is the same: how do you check a contractor COI against your project requirements? The endorsements matter as much as the policy, starting with primary and noncontributory wording.

item.title: Does a project-specific liability policy cover work after the job is built?
item.description: A Texas highway pileup case shows how a liability policy limited to one project's construction work can leave out claims about running the road after it opens.
item.content:encoded:
• Not always. A policy written for one project's construction work may not cover claims about what happens after the project is done, such as operating or maintaining it.
  • In a ruling reported Oct 29, 2026, Liberty Mutual was found to have no duty to defend the builders of a Fort Worth toll road in lawsuits over a 2021 pileup that killed six people.
  • The trial court held that the policy covered bodily injury arising out of work for the project, and that operating and maintaining the road after it opened in 2018 wasn't that work.
  • If a contractor also operates or maintains what it built, check that its coverage reaches that work too, not just the construction phase.

Not always. A liability policy written for one project's construction work can stop short of claims about what happens after the job is built. A Texas highway case reported last week shows how.

The pileup and the policy

On Feb. 11, 2021, a 130-car pileup in a winter storm on I-35W in Fort Worth killed six people and injured about 65, Business Insurance reports. The crash led to dozens of lawsuits against the builders of that stretch of highway, the tollway operator and trucking companies.

The builders, North Tarrant Infrastructure, Ferrovial Construction US and Webber, had a 2013 liability policy from a Liberty Mutual unit for the toll road project. The policy excluded bodily injury arising out of work for any project other than the one it named: rebuilding 6.5 miles of I-35W, building new frontage roads and adding toll lanes. In the district court's words, "the Policy only includes coverage for bodily injury arising out of work conducted for the project."

Why building it wasn't running it

Liberty Mutual defended the builders under a reservation of rights, then sued to get out of the defense. Under Texas's eight-corners rule, the duty to defend turns only on the policy and what the lawsuits allege.

The lawsuits didn't allege the road was built wrong. They alleged failures in operating and maintaining it, including preparing for winter weather. The road opened in 2018, so the district court held that later operation and maintenance couldn't be work "for" a project defined as rebuilding, constructing and expanding the road. Liberty Mutual had no duty to defend.

Business Insurance reports that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit has now affirmed the ruling, and quotes the court calling the policy "clunky and poorly drafted." The district court left one question open: whether Liberty Mutual must pay any judgment. It said that wasn't ripe, since facts at trial could differ from the allegations.

What it means for project requirements

Some projects, like public-private toll roads, have the team that builds them also operate and maintain them. A policy that names a project and its construction work covers that phase. It may not cover the years after.

  1. Read how the policy describes the covered project and the covered work. Narrow descriptions mean narrow coverage.
  2. If a contractor will also operate or maintain the project, ask which policy covers that phase, and get it on file.
  3. Match each phase in your project requirements to a policy that actually reaches it, including completed operations.
  4. Remember a certificate won't show any of this. Get the policy wording or endorsements behind it.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

That's the question behind point 3: does additional insured status cover you after the job is done? For the rest of the certificate, see how to read a certificate of insurance.

item.title: What does "per written contract" mean on a blanket additional insured endorsement?
item.description: Per written contract wording on a blanket additional insured endorsement: whose contract counts, CG 20 33 vs CG 20 38, and what to check on a contractor COI.
item.content:encoded:
• "Per written contract" means the policy adds as an additional insured whoever a written contract requires, instead of naming each party on a schedule.
  • CG 20 33 requires a contract between you and the named insured. CG 20 38 can reach parties further up the contract chain.
  • New York's highest court held in 2018 that "with whom you have agreed" by written contract requires that direct contract.
  • Courts also look at whether the agreement was in writing, signed before the loss, and actually required additional insured status.
  • A certificate doesn't create additional insured status. Get the endorsement and keep the signed contract on file.

"Per written contract" means the policy adds as an additional insured whoever a written contract requires it to add, instead of naming each party on a schedule. That's what makes an endorsement a blanket additional insured endorsement. It's convenient: one endorsement covers every owner and GC a contractor works for. But it only covers you if your project fits the endorsement's exact words, and those words differ more than most people expect.

As IA Magazine put it, "There is no such thing as a blanket additional insured endorsement." ISO offers several automatic forms, and they differ greatly. Insurers write their own versions too. The County of Sonoma's insurance guide notes that many blanket additional insured endorsements are insurer proprietary forms, not ISO forms, and that each one has to be read against the contract.

Whose contract counts under per written contract wording?

The biggest question is whether the endorsement covers only parties the named insured contracted with directly. Lawyers call that privity of contract.

New York's Court of Appeals answered it for one common wording in 2018. In Gilbane Building Co./TDX Construction Corp. v. St. Paul Fire and Marine Insurance Co., a construction manager on a Bellevue Hospital Campus project required each prime contractor to name it as an additional insured. One prime contractor's policy covered "any person or organization with whom you have agreed to add as an additional insured by written contract." The construction manager had no contract of its own with that prime contractor. The court ruled 5-2 that "with whom" meant the written contract had to be with the additional insured, so the construction manager wasn't covered, as Jones Day reported. The prime contract's insurance requirements couldn't rewrite the policy.

Other courts have read similar per written contract language both ways. IRMI reports that an Illinois court found "such person or organization" required a direct written agreement, while federal courts in Maine and Connecticut found similar wording didn't.

What's the difference between CG 20 33 and CG 20 38?

ISO's two construction blanket additional insured forms answer the privity question differently.

CG 20 33 and CG 20 38 compared, per IA Magazine and Jones Day
QuestionCG 20 33CG 20 38
Who it addsParties the named insured has a written construction agreement withThose parties, plus other parties that agreement requires it to add
Privity of contractRequiredNot necessarily required
Covers an owner above the GCOnly with a direct contractYes, if the contract requires it
Jones Day's advice (2018)Avoid this typeConsider CG 20 38 04 13

So when an owner's contract requires the GC to add the owner, and the GC's contracts pass that requirement down, CG 20 38 is the form built to carry the owner along. CG 20 33 covers only the GC that signed with the contractor. Whether either one reaches finished work is a separate question, so check that part of the wording on the contractor COI's endorsement too, and see completed operations additional insured coverage.

Does the contract have to be in writing and signed before the loss?

Per written contract wording can raise three more questions, and IRMI found courts split on each:

  • Is it in writing? Some courts have accepted letters, faxes and proposals. In Atofina v. Continental Casualty (2005), the Texas Supreme Court accepted a written construction proposal. Two New York appellate courts have said an oral agreement could count under some wording.
  • Was it signed in time? Many endorsements require the agreement to be executed before the loss, and IRMI says many courts are inflexible on that. In Empire Builders v. Delos (2010), coverage failed because the agreement came too late.
  • Does it actually require additional insured status? In A.F. Lusi Construction v. Peerless (2004), the Rhode Island Supreme Court found no additional insured agreement because the trade contract's required insurance section was blank. A certificate noting a blanket endorsement didn't fix it.

These fights are still live. In a lawsuit filed in federal court in New York and reported by Insurance Business in July 2026, Berkley alleges Trisura refused to defend a project owner under an endorsement whose schedule read "Per Written Contract." Part of the dispute, as reported, is whether a purchase order's insurance exhibit counts as a written contract. The allegations haven't been decided.

How do you check per written contract wording on a contractor COI?

You check per written contract wording by reading the endorsement, not the certificate:

  1. Get the endorsement. Jones Day notes that additional insured status is created only by an endorsement the insurer issues. Ask for the declarations and schedule of forms too.
  2. Find the form number and edition. CG 20 33, CG 20 38 or an insurer's own form each read differently.
  3. Read the wording. Look for "with whom," "such person or organization" and any execution or timing requirement.
  4. Check it reaches every party your project requirements name, including owners who don't contract with that contractor directly.
  5. Keep the signed contract, with its insurance requirements, on file next to the endorsement and the contractor COI.
  6. Recheck at renewal, when forms can change.

Watch: What does additional insured mean? The sixth-grade version (0:33). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

IA Magazine's advice to agents applies to you as the reader: a certificate should list the endorsement and its edition date, and you should get a copy. "Always read the COI like a person with no insurance background would."

What else should your project requirements say?

A blanket additional insured endorsement is only as good as the contract behind it. Write your project requirements so the contract does the work: name every party that needs additional insured status, require it for ongoing and completed operations, and require it to be primary and noncontributory. Sign the contract before work starts. Then check that your state's rules allow what you're asking for, using the contractor COI requirements for your state.

Forsured reads the endorsements behind each contractor COI and flags per written contract wording that doesn't reach every party your project requirements name, for the life of the job. item.title: Can parametric insurance cover weather delays on a construction project?
item.description: Builder's risk pays for physical damage, not for days lost to cold, heat or wind. A CRC panel explained how parametric cover fills that gap.
item.content:encoded:
• Yes. Parametric policies pay a set amount when a measured trigger is hit, such as a cold, heat, wind, rain or snow threshold, so they can cover weather that halts work without damaging it.
  • Traditional builder's risk covers physical damage only, so lost days, overtime and schedule pressure from weather usually fall on the contractor.
  • Panelists at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference said cover can be tailored to specific operations, such as cold only on concrete pour days or wind only on crane days.
  • Payouts can be used for any purpose, such as funding overtime after a delay.

Yes, it can. Builder's risk insurance pays when weather damages the work. It doesn't pay when weather stops the work. Parametric insurance fills that gap by paying a set amount when a measured trigger is hit at the site, such as a temperature, wind speed or rainfall threshold, whether or not anything was damaged.

That was the case a panel made on Tuesday at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor, as reported by Business Insurance.

The gap builder's risk leaves

Weather stops work long before it breaks anything. Rose Hall, founder of construction risk advisory firm RH Business Ventures, said a day below 40 degrees could cut poured concrete's strength by 50%, and winds above 20 mph can make some crane operations unsafe. Neither shows up as a builder's risk claim.

"Contractors are just absorbing (non-covered weather losses), mostly silently," Hall said.

The panel also pointed to the human cost. Heat-related worker fatalities have risen, and builders often feel pressure to keep working through extreme conditions to stay on schedule.

Cover the days that stop your work

Parametric cover doesn't have to insure every storm. Gary Kaplan, former president of construction at AXA XL, put it this way: "The goal is not to cover every weather event. It is to cover the specific events that stop your specific operations at your specific location."

That means a policy can be shaped around the job:

  • Cold, but only on concrete pour days.
  • Wind, but only on crane days.
  • Payouts that can be used for anything, such as overtime to recover a delay.

Chris Smith, a senior director at the Baldwin Group, said larger builders could use it across a portfolio, and captive owners could use a payout to fund the captive's deductible after a catastrophic event. "To me, this is schedule guardianship," he said.

A better weather number for the bid

Contractors usually set weather allowances in bids from rough estimates. Hall noted that a 10-year average can hide large swings from one year to the next. Kaplan proposed a "zero-weather-day bid," built on site-specific weather estimates, that could give a bidder an edge.

What it means for project requirements

If parametric cover starts showing up in project requirements, it becomes one more line to verify, with its own triggers, limits and named site. As with every coverage, the certificate is only the summary. The policy terms are what pay. Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

The question behind it applies to every line on the certificate: is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage? For the full review, see how to read a certificate of insurance.

item.title: What does primary and noncontributory mean on a contractor COI?
item.description: Primary and noncontributory decides whose policy pays first when a contractor's work causes a loss. What it means, how CG 20 01 creates it, and what to check.
item.content:encoded:
• Primary and noncontributory sets the order in which overlapping policies respond: the contractor's policy pays first, without seeking contribution from the additional insured's own policy.
  • Without noncontributory wording, two primary policies can end up sharing defense costs and damages.
  • It's created by an endorsement on the contractor's general liability policy, such as ISO's CG 20 01. The ACORD 25 has no field for it.
  • CG 20 01 applies only when a written contract requires it, and only to the general liability policy, not an attached umbrella.

Read the insurance section of almost any construction contract and you'll find the same phrase: additional insured coverage "on a primary and noncontributory basis." It's so common it reads like boilerplate. It isn't. Primary and noncontributory decides whose insurance pays first when a contractor's work causes a loss, and whether your own policy gets pulled in to share it.

What does primary and noncontributory mean?

IRMI defines primary and noncontributory as a term used in contract insurance requirements "to stipulate the order in which multiple policies triggered by the same loss are to respond." Split it in two:

  • Primary: the contractor's policy must pay before other applicable policies, including the additional insured's own.
  • Noncontributory: the contractor's policy pays without seeking contribution from other policies that also claim to be primary.

The County of Sonoma's insurance guide puts the primary half plainly: "The vendor's policy pays before the additional insured's policy or self-insurance are involved." The County requires additional insured coverage on a primary and noncontributory basis so that its own self-insured retention isn't touched until the limits of the contractor's policy are used up.

How does the other insurance condition split a loss?

Every general liability policy has an other insurance condition that decides how it shares a loss with other policies. Left alone, that condition can split the claim. Sonoma's guide walks through the outcomes:

How the contractor's and the additional insured's policies respond, per the County of Sonoma
Additional insured wordingHow the two policies respond
Neither primary nor noncontributory, both policies excessThey become contributing primary insurance and share defense costs and damages
Primary only, both policies primaryThey become contributing primary insurance and share the loss
Primary and noncontributoryThe contractor's policy pays first, without contribution from yours, until its limits are exhausted

So "primary" on its own isn't enough. If your policy is also primary, the two policies contribute. It takes both words, primary and noncontributory, to keep your policy out of a claim the contractor's work caused.

Which endorsement creates primary and noncontributory?

Like additional insured status, primary and noncontributory is created by policy wording, not by the certificate. The ACORD 25 has no field for primary, noncontributory or other insurance wording, and it says the certificate confers no rights on the holder. A note in the description of operations box doesn't change the policy.

What a contractor COI can do is point you to the right paper. IA Magazine advises agents to list the endorsement and its edition date on the certificate and give the holder a copy, rather than typing a general statement of coverage. Ask for the same on every contractor COI: the form number, the edition, and the endorsement itself.

In 2013 ISO introduced an optional endorsement for it, CG 20 01, "Primary and Noncontributory, Other Insurance Condition." Claims Journal explained that it was introduced in response to wording in many construction contracts, and that it alters the other insurance condition to state that additional insured coverage is provided on a primary and noncontributory basis. Whether an additional premium applies is up to the insurance carrier. Many carriers use CG 20 01 or their own version, and Jones Day recommends that owners and GCs require CG 20 01 04 13.

Primary and noncontributory rides on additional insured status, so it's only as good as the additional insured endorsement it modifies. Check both endorsements together, including completed operations coverage after the job is done.

When does CG 20 01 apply?

CG 20 01 comes with two conditions, as Claims Journal lists them. It applies only when:

  1. The additional insured is a named insured on another policy, and
  2. A written contract or agreement requires the contractor's policy to be primary and not to seek contribution from other insurance available to the additional insured.

Missing contract language means missing primary and noncontributory coverage. Write it into your project requirements, and make sure the contract is signed before work starts.

If an owner requires primary and noncontributory coverage from you, pass the same requirement down to every contractor on the job, in the same words. Public owners like the County of Sonoma require it as a matter of course. A gap between what the owner asks of you and what you ask of your contractors lands on your own policy, and the contractor COI won't show you that gap unless you compare the endorsement against both contracts.

Does primary and noncontributory cover the umbrella?

Not under CG 20 01. Claims Journal says the endorsement "applies to the CGL only, not any umbrella that may be attached." If your project requirements call for primary and noncontributory umbrella or excess coverage, the umbrella needs to say so in its own wording. Read the umbrella policy's form, or get the contractor's broker to confirm in writing which policies carry primary and noncontributory wording.

How do you check primary and noncontributory on a contractor COI?

You check primary and noncontributory on a contractor COI by reading past the certificate to the endorsements:

  1. Confirm your project requirements actually call for primary and noncontributory, and on which policies: general liability, auto, umbrella.
  2. Ask for the endorsement, not just the certificate. Note the form number and edition, such as CG 20 01 04 13.
  3. Check that it covers the parties your requirements name: owner, lender, GC and others.
  4. Check the umbrella or excess policy separately when the requirements extend to it.
  5. Confirm the written contract requiring primary and noncontributory coverage is signed and on file.
  6. Recheck at renewal. Endorsements change when policies renew, and forms keep evolving. "Evolving insurance endorsements" were the backdrop for Cullen and Dykman's session on additional insured endorsements at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference.

Two related clauses usually sit next to primary and noncontributory in the contract's insurance section: a waiver of subrogation and a per project aggregate. Check them in the same pass.

It's one line in the contract and one endorsement on the policy. Forsured checks the primary and noncontributory endorsement behind every contractor COI, against each project's requirements, for the life of the job. item.title: What we heard at our first IRMI Construction Risk Conference
item.description: Forsured spent IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference talking COIs with brokers, carriers and contractors. Five things we heard, and what we're doing about them.
item.content:encoded:
• Forsured spent IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor meeting brokers, carriers and contractors about contractor COIs.
  • The loudest complaint: today's COI tools throw too many red alerts and reject certificates over small issues without explaining what actually matters.
  • Brokers and carriers want contractor COI data they can bring to renewals and share with clients, not more paperwork.
  • Neutral wording, "project requirements" and "contractor COIs", landed with general contractors and trade contractors alike, so that's how we talk now.

This week Forsured showed up at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference at the Gaylord National in National Harbor. It was our first CRC. We weren't on the sponsor list and we didn't have a booth. We had a mix of black and white Forsured polos, an independent field guide to the conference, a short video about catching the COI gap, and one question for everyone we met: what happens to a contractor COI after it's filed?

The answers were consistent enough that we want to share them. Nobody below is named, because these were hallway conversations, not interviews.

1. Too many red alerts, not enough answers

The complaint we heard most came from people already paying for COI tracking. Their tools flag everything. Certificates get rejected over small formatting issues, contractors get frustrated, and the alerts that matter (a lapsed policy, an umbrella below the project requirement, an additional insured endorsement without completed operations) get lost in the noise.

Watch: One platform for GCs, contractors and their brokers (0:53). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

What they want is a review that reads the certificate and the endorsements the way a risk manager would, ranks what actually exposes the project, and says why.

2. Brokers want data for renewals

Brokers told us the same thing in different words: show me what my client's contracts actually required last year, and how often their contractors fell short. With umbrella and excess rates still rising (WTW expects another 5% to 15% in 2027), walking into a renewal with that data is worth more than another stack of certificates.

3. Carriers care how contractors manage the trades they hire

Underwriters are paying attention to contractor management. Carrier teams we spoke with were interested in tools they could point their construction insureds to, because a contractor that checks every COI against project requirements is a better risk.

4. Big projects are still run on spreadsheets

Some of the largest projects represented at CRC still track contractor insurance in spreadsheets and inboxes. Certificates arrive in different formats from different countries, and the people responsible know they can't see the whole picture.

5. The words matter

We came in using the general contractor's shorthand for the paperwork. By the end of day 1 we'd switched to "project requirements" and "contractor COIs." The neutral wording works for general contractors, trade contractors and owners alike, and it describes the real job: every contractor, checked against what the project requires.

What's next

We're following up with everyone who asked to see Forsured on their own paperwork. If we didn't get to meet you at the Gaylord, the offer is the same: a free COI risk check, no strings attached. Send one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two to hello@forsured.ai, and we'll walk you through every gap we find.

We'll also keep writing here every weekday about what's moving in construction insurance and contractor COI compliance. Thank you to IRMI and everyone in National Harbor who stopped to talk.

If you're starting from scratch, begin with two questions: how do you check a contractor COI against your project requirements? And is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage?

item.title: Is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage? Why a COI alone isn't enough
item.description: A certificate of insurance isn't proof of coverage. Here's what a contractor COI can hide, what courts say, and what to check against your project requirements.
item.content:encoded:
• Most courts won't let a certificate holder rely on a certificate that contradicts the policy. A few states, Ohio among them, have gone the other way.
  • Exclusions, endorsement wording and aggregate rules never appear on the certificate, and they're where claims get denied.
  • Policies change mid-job: a contractor COI that passed in March can fail by July.
  • Check every contractor COI against the project's own requirements, get the endorsements, and keep checking for the life of the job.

Every general contractor has a folder of contractor COIs. Most were looked at once, by someone in a hurry, when the contractor was onboarded. That folder feels like proof of coverage. It isn't, and the reasons are written on the certificate itself.

What is a certificate of insurance, and what does it prove?

A certificate of insurance proves that certain policies existed on the day it was issued, and not much more. IRMI defines it as a document giving evidence that certain general types of insurance have been bought, with the coverage types and limits. That's the whole job: evidence, on one date.

Watch: Is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage? Read the fine print (0:46). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

The standard ACORD 25 says so on its face. The 2025/12 edition is "issued as a matter of information only and confers no rights upon the certificate holder," and it doesn't amend, extend or alter the coverage of the policies listed. When the certificate and the policy disagree, the policy wins.

Why isn't a certificate of insurance proof of coverage?

A certificate of insurance isn't proof of coverage because courts mostly treat it the way the form describes itself. Koley Jessen notes that most courts won't let a certificate holder rely on a certificate whose contents are wrong. Taft points to a minority view: Ohio's Supreme Court in Pedler v. Aetna (1986) held an insurer to the coverage a certificate described. That split is a reason to check, not a reason to rely.

Risk Management Magazine collected the cases that show what goes wrong in practice:

  • A policy was canceled for nonpayment after the certificate was issued, the certificate holder wasn't told, and it couldn't claim under the policy.
  • A certificate and policy both named an owner as additional insured, but the endorsement covered only the named insured's own work. A different trade caused the fire, so there was no duty to defend.
  • A certificate said a company was covered under a roofer's policy. The court found the policy gave no such coverage.

This is general information, not legal advice. How your state treats a certificate is a question for your attorney.

What can a contractor COI hide?

A contractor COI hides most of what decides a claim. The one-page form summarizes policies that run dozens of pages, and the details that matter most never make it onto the page.

Watch: What is a certificate of insurance (COI)? Basically a selfie (0:32). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

What a contractor COI shows, and what actually decides coverage
ItemWhat the certificate showsWhat decides coverage
Additional insuredA checked ADDL INSD boxThe endorsement form and its wording
Completed operationsUsually nothingWhether the endorsement covers work after the job
Waiver of subrogationA checked SUBR WVD boxThe waiver endorsement
ExclusionsNothingThe policy: height limits, residential work, labor law, EIFS and more
AggregateA box for policy, project or locationWhether a per project aggregate endorsement is attached
LimitsThe amounts you asked forThe policy limits, less paid claims
DatesThe term on the day it was issuedAny cancellation or change since

The 2025/12 edition adds a note worth knowing. It says the limits shown include amounts requested by the certificate holder and may not reflect higher policy limits, and that limits may have been reduced by paid claims. A certificate that shows your required limit may show only your required limit.

Which exclusions never show on a certificate of insurance?

Exclusions never show on a certificate of insurance, and they're where proof of coverage most often falls apart. The coverages grid lists policy types and limits. It doesn't list what the policy carves out. Common construction exclusions include work above a certain height, residential or condo projects, exterior insulation and finish systems (EIFS), and action-over claims under New York's labor law, where an injured worker sues the owner or GC. A roofer with a height exclusion or a framer with a residential exclusion can hand you a clean certificate for exactly the work the policy won't cover.

The only proof of coverage for those risks is the policy itself: the declarations, the forms schedule and the endorsements. On a high-risk trade, ask the broker to confirm in writing that no exclusion applies to your project's scope of work.

Does a checked additional insured box make you an additional insured?

A checked additional insured box doesn't make you an additional insured. The ACORD 25 says that if the certificate holder is an additional insured, the policy must have additional insured provisions or be endorsed, and that a statement on the certificate doesn't replace the endorsement.

The endorsement's wording matters too. Forms change often, a point Christopher Ruggiero of Cullen and Dykman made at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference: the coverage you negotiate only holds if the endorsement on the policy matches it. Check that additional insured status covers completed operations, and whether it applies only where a written contract requires it.

What should you check against your project requirements instead?

Instead of relying on a contractor COI, check it against the project's own requirements and get the documents behind it:

  1. Start from the project requirements, not a generic checklist. Each owner, lender and contract writes its own project requirements, with its own limits and wording.
  2. Read each certificate of insurance line by line against those project requirements: coverages, limits, dates, and a named insured that matches the contracting entity.
  3. Ask for the endorsements the project requirements depend on, and read the form numbers and wording.
  4. Check state rules on workers' comp and anti-indemnity in the COI requirements for your state, and whether the aggregate must be per project.
  5. Track renewals and expirations, because a certificate doesn't tell you when a policy is canceled.

Forsured checks each contractor COI and its endorsement forms against the requirements set for that project, flags each gap for your team to approve, and keeps checking for the life of the job.

Why do carriers care how you check contractor COIs?

Carriers care because a weak contractor COI program shows up in a GC's own losses. WTW says underwriters give favorable consideration to contractors with strong management of the trade partners they hire, and it expects umbrella and excess rates to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027. That's exactly the line where trade contractors trim, and exactly the line a file of unchecked certificates won't catch. Run a free COI risk check on one project to see what yours would show.

item.title: 3 takeaways from day 2 of IRMI's Construction Risk Conference
item.description: Additional insured endorsements, prequalification as a snapshot, and insurance data you can't search. What we were digging into on day 2 at IRMI CRC 2026.
item.content:encoded:
• Additional insured coverage only holds if the endorsement on the contractor's policy matches the project requirements, and endorsement forms keep changing.
  • Prequalification checks insurance once. Policies renew, lapse and get re-endorsed mid-project, so compliance has to be checked continuously.
  • Contractor COIs stored as PDFs can't be trended, audited or shared with a broker or carrier at renewal.

Day 2 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference is a wrap. Three things we were digging into on Tuesday.

1. The endorsement is the contract's last line of defense

Tuesday opened with "Decoding Additional Insured Endorsements for Successful Contractual Risk Transfer," led by Christopher Ruggiero, partner and construction litigation chair at Cullen and Dykman. His preview made a point every GC should hear: as claim costs rise, the indemnity and additional insured coverage you negotiate is harder to secure, because the endorsement forms keep changing.

The coverage you negotiated only holds if the endorsement on the contractor's policy actually matches your project requirements. A checked box on a COI doesn't tell you that. The form number and its wording do.

2. Prequalification is a snapshot. Insurance is a moving target.

"The Prequalification Puzzle" was on Tuesday's agenda, and it's a good reminder of how much happens after a contractor clears prequal. A contractor COI that passed in March can be out of compliance by July. Policies renew with new terms, lapse for nonpayment and get re-endorsed mid-project.

Watch: What is a certificate of insurance (COI)? Basically a selfie (0:32). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

Prequalification answers "can this firm do the work?" It was never built to answer "is this firm covered today, for this project?"

3. Insurance data you can't search is its own risk

Contractor COIs sitting as PDFs in an inbox can't be trended, audited or shared with your broker or carrier when renewal comes around. "When Data Becomes Risk" was on the afternoon agenda, and that's the version of it we see most: the information exists, but nobody can answer a simple question like "which of our active contractors carry less umbrella than the job requires?"

Structured COI data turns that into a two-minute answer, and it's the same data a carrier wants to see when it asks how you manage the trades you hire.

If you want that answer for one of your own projects, start with one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two.

The question underneath is simple: how do you check a contractor COI against your project requirements? For the endorsements behind the certificate, start with completed operations additional insured coverage.

item.title: IRMI is rewriting its design-build risk and insurance guide
item.description: IRMI picked American Global to rewrite its Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide. What the update covers, and what design-build means for contractor COI review.
item.content:encoded:
• IRMI selected brokerage American Global to rewrite its Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide, edited by IRMI's Megan Jolly.
  • The update covers progressive design-build, risk allocation, indemnification, limits of liability, professional liability, project-specific coverage and bonding.
  • On design-build work, check contractor COIs for professional liability wherever a contractor carries design responsibility, not just general liability.

The International Risk Management Institute (IRMI) has picked American Global, a construction and infrastructure risk and insurance brokerage, to rewrite its long-running Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide. The team includes Caryn Maxfield, Ante Petricevic, François Wasselin and Giovanni Bach, with IRMI's Megan Jolly editing, according to the October 23 announcement.

What the update covers

The rewrite is meant to catch up with how design-build is delivered today, including progressive design-build. It covers contractual risk allocation, indemnification, limits of liability, professional liability insurance, project-specific coverage and bonding.

Why it matters for contractor COIs

Design-build shifts design responsibility to the builder's side of the contract. That has a direct effect on what a compliant contractor COI looks like:

  • Professional liability enters the picture. A design-builder, and any trade contractor doing delegated design on mechanical, electrical, structural steel or curtain wall scopes, may need professional liability that a general liability policy won't provide.
  • Requirements differ by role. The same project can need different coverage from a designer, a design-builder and a build-only trade contractor. One template for every firm misses that.
  • Project-specific programs change the checklist. When an owner or contractor buys project-specific coverage, contractor COIs have to be checked against what the program does and doesn't cover.

WTW's 2027 outlook expects contractor's professional liability to run flat to up 5% on annual programs and flat to up 10% on project-specific policies, so the coverage is available. The job is making sure the contractors who need it actually carry it, at the limits the project requires.

IRMI's guides are a standard reference for construction risk teams, and this one is worth reading when it lands.

Whatever the delivery method, the question is the same: how do you check each contractor COI against the project requirements for its role? A certificate alone won't answer it, because a certificate of insurance isn't proof of coverage.

item.title: How to read a certificate of insurance: checking a contractor COI against your project requirements
item.description: How to read a certificate of insurance field by field, and check a contractor COI against your project requirements: limits, dates, endorsements and gaps.
item.content:encoded:
• The ACORD 25 says it confers no rights on the certificate holder. The policy and its endorsements decide coverage.
  • The 2025/12 edition notes that limits shown can include only the amounts the holder requested, and may have been reduced by paid claims.
  • Most gaps sit in five places: umbrella limits, completed operations, the aggregate, entity names and expiration dates.
  • Send the broker the exact requirement and the exact line that misses it. Specific asks get fixed in days.

Knowing how to read a certificate of insurance is mostly knowing what it can't prove. The certificate summarizes a contractor's coverage on one page. Your job is to hold that summary against the project requirements for this job, line by line, and then ask for the documents behind anything that matters.

What do you need before you read a certificate of insurance?

Learning how to read a certificate of insurance starts with the contract, not the certificate. Pull the insurance section of the subcontract or the project's insurance requirements exhibit. A contractor COI can only pass or fail against something written down. For this project, note:

  • Each required coverage: general liability, auto, workers' compensation and employer's liability, umbrella or excess, and anything trade-specific like professional or pollution liability
  • The minimum limit for each, and whether the umbrella must follow form
  • Required endorsements: additional insured for ongoing and completed operations, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory
  • Who must be named: owner, lender, GC and anyone else the contract lists
  • How long completed operations coverage must last after the job, and whether the aggregate must apply per project

Watch: Check your contractor's insurance every job, even the ones you trust (0:37). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

Requirements differ by owner, lender and contract, so a template from the last job is a guess, not a standard.

What does each ACORD 25 field tell you?

The ACORD 25 is the standard liability certificate, published by ACORD. The current edition is 2025/12 (the form as posted by the New York Department of Financial Services). Here's how to read a certificate of insurance on that form, field by field.

Watch: Is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage? Read the fine print (0:46). Steve Massei, a Bay Area general contractor. Steve is an owner of Forsured and its Chief Construction Officer.

ACORD 25 fields and what to check against your project requirements
ACORD 25 fieldWhat it showsWhat to check
DateWhen the certificate was issuedA certificate from last year proves nothing about today
ProducerThe agent or broker who issued itWho you'll ask for fixes; not proof of coverage
InsuredThe contractor's legal name and addressMatches the entity on the contract, not a parent, DBA or sister company
Insurers A to F, NAIC #The carriers behind each policyReal, named carriers; the NAIC number lets you look them up
INSR LTRWhich insurer writes each lineEvery required line has a carrier
ADDL INSDAdditional insured is claimed on that lineA claim only; ask for the endorsement form
SUBR WVDWaiver of subrogation is claimedSame: ask for the endorsement
Policy number, EFF, EXPEach policy and its datesIn force for the whole job; note every expiration
LimitsEach occurrence, aggregates, products and completed operationsAt or above every required limit
Gen'l aggregate applies perPolicy, project or locationPer project, if your contract requires it
Umbrella or excessLimit, occurrence or claims-madeMeets the requirement; follow form if required
Workers' comp and E.L.Statutory coverage and employer's liability limitsCovers the states where the work is
Description of operationsFree text, often the project and named partiesNames this project and your contract where required
Certificate holderWho asked for the certificateYour correct legal entity
CancellationHow notice of cancellation worksNotice follows the policy, not the certificate

Forsured reads the certificate and the endorsement forms attached to each contractor COI, checks them against the requirements set for that project, and flags every line that falls short.

What doesn't a contractor COI tell you?

A contractor COI on the ACORD 25 doesn't create coverage. The form says it's issued as a matter of information only and confers no rights on the certificate holder, and that it doesn't amend, extend or alter the policies. That's why a COI alone isn't enough.

Three lines on the form are worth knowing by heart:

  • The additional insured note. If the certificate holder is an additional insured, the policy must have additional insured provisions or be endorsed. A statement on the certificate doesn't replace the endorsement.
  • The limits note. The 2025/12 edition says the limits shown include amounts requested by the certificate holder and may not reflect policy limits above those requested. It also says limits may have been reduced by paid claims. A certificate that shows your required limit may show only your required limit.
  • The cancellation box. "Should any of the above described policies be cancelled before the expiration date thereof, notice will be delivered in accordance with the policy provisions." The certificate holder isn't promised a notice. See how to find out when a policy is canceled.

What are the most common gaps on a contractor COI?

The most common contractor COI gaps look fine on a quick read. Anyone who knows how to read a certificate of insurance checks the same five places every time.

  1. Umbrella or excess below the requirement. Project requirements often ask for more than a trade contractor carries on its standard program.
  2. Additional insured that stops when the job does. CG 20 10 covers ongoing operations. You need completed operations too, usually CG 20 37 or a blanket form that includes it. See completed operations additional insured.
  3. An aggregate shared across every job. When the "applies per" box says policy, one bad claim elsewhere can empty it. The fix is a designated construction project aggregate endorsement, which IRMI defines. See per project aggregate.
  4. A named insured that doesn't match the contract. The wrong entity on the certificate means you can't be sure the right one is covered.
  5. Missing waiver or primary wording. A checked SUBR WVD box isn't a waiver. Ask for the waiver of subrogation endorsement and the primary and noncontributory endorsement.

How do state rules change what you check on a certificate of insurance?

State rules change which certificate of insurance lines you can rely on. Workers' compensation thresholds, monopolistic workers' comp states, license insurance minimums and anti-indemnity statutes that limit additional insured requirements all vary. Check the contractor COI requirements for your state before you write the project requirements for limits or endorsements on a job there.

How do you get a gap on a contractor COI fixed?

You get a gap on a contractor COI fixed by asking the contractor's broker for one specific change. The review checklist from ISO gives the same advice: put the deficiency in writing and get a corrected certificate before work starts. A short note works best:

Hi, for the Main Street project our project requirements call for umbrella limits of $5 million each occurrence and additional insured coverage for completed operations. The certificate dated October 2 shows $2 million umbrella and CG 20 10 only. Can you send an updated certificate and the CG 20 37 or equivalent endorsement?

Specific asks get fixed in days. Vague ones ("please send an updated COI") come back with the same certificate. And a review is only as good as its date, so recheck at every renewal and before every expiration on the job. Knowing how to read a certificate of insurance once isn't the same as knowing the contractor is covered today. Run a free COI risk check on one project to see what a full review finds.

item.title: 3 takeaways from day 1 of IRMI's Construction Risk Conference
item.description: Crowded bids and thin margins, umbrella rates still rising, and contractor management turning into an underwriting factor. What stuck with us from day 1 at IRMI CRC 2026.
item.content:encoded:
• Bids are crowded: ABC chief economist Anirban Basu says jobs that once drew 2 to 4 bids now draw as many as 12 to 16, and about a third of contractors expect margins to shrink.
  • WTW expects umbrella and excess rates to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027, and brokers want renewal data on how often contracts demand high umbrella limits.
  • Carriers give favorable consideration to strong management of the contractors a firm hires, so contractor COI compliance is becoming an underwriting story.

Day 1 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor is in the books. Here are the three things that stuck with us from Monday, and what each one means for anyone collecting contractor COIs.

1. Margins are thin, and bids are crowded

Anirban Basu, chief economist at Associated Builders and Contractors, opened CRC's Monday general session. His recent numbers, reported by Construction Dive, set the tone: projects that once drew two to four bids are now drawing as many as 12 to 16, and about 32% of contractors surveyed expect profit margins to decline over the next year, up from 26% in July.

When the low bid wins, a contractor's insurance gap isn't a paperwork problem. It's a margin problem. A trade contractor that trimmed its umbrella to sharpen a number is the one whose gap lands back on the GC's program after a loss.

2. Umbrella is where the pain is

WTW expects umbrella and excess rates for construction to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027, the same range it gives auto liability, while general liability runs flat to up 10%.

A broker we sat down with asked for something simple: show me how many of last year's contracts required a high umbrella limit, so I can walk into renewal with data instead of guesses. That data exists in every GC's contractor COI file. It just isn't searchable when the certificates are PDFs in an inbox.

3. Contractor management is becoming an underwriting factor

WTW's outlook says carriers give favorable underwriting consideration to firms with strong management of the trades they hire, alongside loss experience and fleet controls. "When Compliance Isn't Coverage" was on Monday's agenda for a reason: a contractor COI in a file isn't proof of coverage, and underwriters know it.

For a GC, that turns COI review from back-office cleanup into something you can show a carrier at renewal: every contractor checked against project requirements, every gap tracked to a fix.

Want to see what your own contractor COI file would tell a carrier? That's what our free COI risk check is for.

Underwriters are asking the question behind it: is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage? It isn't, and how to read a certificate of insurance shows what to check instead.

item.title: What the 2027 construction insurance outlook means for contractor COIs
item.description: WTW forecasts construction umbrella and excess rates up 5% to 15% in 2027. Here's the full outlook by line, and why it raises the stakes on contractor COI review.
item.content:encoded:
• WTW's 2027 outlook for construction: umbrella and excess up 5% to 15%, auto up 5% to 15%, general liability flat to up 10%, workers' compensation flat to up 5%.
  • Lead umbrella and excess on wrap-up programs (OCIPs and CCIPs) is also expected up 5% to 15%.
  • When umbrella costs rise, trade contractors are tempted to carry less than project requirements demand, so umbrella is the line to check first on every contractor COI.
  • Carriers favor firms with strong management of the contractors they hire, which makes a clean contractor COI record useful at renewal.

WTW published its Insurance Marketplace Realities 2027 report for construction on October 1. The headline for anyone managing contractor COIs: most lines are steady, and the expensive one keeps getting more expensive.

The outlook by line

CoverageWTW 2027 forecast
Umbrella and excess liabilityUp 5% to 15%
Auto liabilityUp 5% to 15%
General liabilityFlat to up 10%
Workers' compensationFlat to up 5%
Project-specific builders risk (non-high hazard)Down 2.5% to up 2.5%
Master builders riskDown 5% to up 5%
Contractor's professional liability (annual)Flat to up 5%
Wrap-ups (OCIP and CCIP), lead umbrella and excessUp 5% to 15%

Umbrella has been the pressure point for years

This isn't new. Back in 2021, ENR reported that umbrella and excess renewals were costing contractors 50% to 100% more, as carriers raised prices, cut limits and raised attachment points. Rates have cooled since then, but umbrella keeps rising faster than the rest of the program.

Why that shows up in your contractor COIs

Project requirements rarely bend to the market. If the contract calls for a $10 million umbrella, it calls for $10 million whether the trade contractor's renewal went up 5% or 15%.

Put that next to a bidding market where, as Construction Dive reported from ABC's Anirban Basu, jobs that once drew 2 to 4 bids are drawing 12 to 16. Thin margins and rising umbrella costs push in the same direction: carry less, and hope nobody checks.

So check umbrella first. On every contractor COI, confirm the umbrella or excess limit meets the project requirement, that it follows form over the underlying policies the contract requires, and that it won't expire before the work is done.

So the question for each contractor on your jobs is whether its umbrella, aggregates and endorsements still match your project requirements. Start with how to read a certificate of insurance, and check the per project aggregate while you're there.

The upside at your own renewal

WTW notes that carriers give favorable underwriting consideration to strong management of the trades a firm hires. A record showing every contractor checked against project requirements, with each gap tracked to a fix, is the kind of evidence an underwriter can use. A folder of unread certificates isn't.
